speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is becoming painfully evident that this government does not give a darn about housing and people. In the past three years we have had three ministers, countless studies, reviews, conferences and more bafflegab. The bottom line is that we have received nothing but cuts, cuts and more cuts to co-op housing, to social housing, to public housing and absolutely zero for home buyers and home builders.
The homeless are growing in numbers, the waiting lists for affordable housing have grown by the thousands. Thousands of workers are out of work and the government dawdles while people suffer more.
The Canadian Home Builders' Association, the Canadian Housing Renewal Association, the Federation of Canadian Municipalities and the Co-Op Housing Federation all call unanimously on this government for a national housing policy, for national leadership on housing and for the Conservatives to be part of the solution, not part of the problem.
Mr. Speaker, this government has the unmitigated gall to spend $375,000 for a dog house. The real question is this. Is this government's housing policies going to the dogs?

Mr. Speaker, in mid-March of this year, I orally warned the now Minister of Fisheries and Oceans that I anticipated unusually difficult ice conditions in Newfoundland.
On May 9,1 wrote the minister again warning him that income for fisherpersons could well be deferred for about a month because of the severe ice accumulation, and I urged him to encourage his colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration, to implement contingencies for this.
Unemployment insurance ran out for fishermen on May 18. From then until now, the extension of UI has been granted on a piecemeal, gradual basis to groups of fishermen from area to area, from week to week. During that period of time, my office made 25 consultative calls with DFO and I wrote two other letters.
Last night, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans announced that all fishermen would be eligible for compensation. In this monthly interval, despite our warnings and advocations, great anxiety has been caused to fishermen and their families, many of whom have had no other source of income since the middle of May.
While we are grateful that this compensation package has finally been approved for all, I would ask the government that should this ever be the case again, that decisions be made earlier, especially when there are warnings and this unnecessary pain, worry and anxiety to those engaged in the primary industry in Newfoundland, be avoided.

Mr. Speaker, community leaders from across Canada will be brought together to improve dialogue and communications among Canadians as a result of funding from the Secretary of State in support of the initiative of the Federation of Canadian Municipalities.
The Federation of Canadian Municipalities is a national organization of some 600 municipalities representing more than 70 per cent of the Canadian population. The federation has been a force for national unity for a long time, and this program will play a positive role in promoting better understanding and fostering dialogue among Canadians from different parts of the country. These programs and efforts are important contributions to Canadian life, because strong and progressive communities are essential to the over-all prosperity and happiness of the country.

The funding from the Secretary of State Department will help the FCM undertake a six-month pilot project for an exchange program in the latter half of 1991.

Mr. Speaker, the threatened closure or downsizing of CFB Shilo by the Department of National Defence would be yet another blow to the economy of Manitoba, from a government seemingly determined to bring it to its knees.
After major reductions to Kapyong Barracks and the transfer of the Second Princess Patricia's Light Infantry from Winnipeg to Edmonton, and the devastating loss of the forces base in the town of Portage la Prairie, it now seems that the government is intent on spreading the misery to Brandon.
CFB Shilo has been invaluable to the department as a training base. It is also the provinces third largest employer outside of Winnipeg and its closing would affect nearly 1,700 military and civilian jobs in the area. Shilo contributes over $110 million annually to the local economy and the spin-off effects from its closure would be disastrous to Brandon and the surrounding area.
We have learned that the troops on the base would in all likelihood be transferred to CFB Suffield, yet another move by this government to build up Alberta at the expense of Manitoba.
I call on the federal government and the new Minister of National Defence to refrain from inflicting further damage on Manitoba's economy.

Mr. Speaker, since today is the last day before the summer recess, I
June 19, 1991
would like to take this opportunity to wish all Quebecers a happy Saint-Jean-Baptiste Day.
Mr. Speaker, I think it would be appropriate to recall what was said 35 years ago by historian Arnold Toynbee, internationally known as one of the greatest historians of this century, when he was a guest speaker at McGill University in Montreal. On this particular occasion, he said that when the Archangel Gabriel sounded the trumpet on the last day, there were two peoples that would definitely be around to hear him: the Chinese and the French Canadians.
I thought he made his point very eloquently and in fact, there is a lot of truth in this when we look at how Quebec, first known as New France, developed since the sixteenth century. French Canadians are indeed here to stay.

Mr. Speaker, June 24, 1991 marked an important date for Canadian trade. In a unanimous decision, the final bilateral dispute panel of the Canada-United States Free Trade Agreement ruled in favour of Canada's pork producers and exporters. The decision will mean millions of dollars in recouped countervail duties for our pork exporters.
This decision reaffirms the success of the free trade agreement and once again proves the anti-free trade Liberals and NDP are dead wrong. The Americans tried their utmost to maintain the status quo but they failed.
United States trade representative Carla Hills stated: "We used the rules that were in place. We got a decision and now we will have to live with it".
Contrary to the naysayers, this demonstrates that the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement is sound and that the dispute settlement mechanism has been tested and proven sound.

Mr. Speaker, eastern Ontario and southern Ontario are the only areas in Canada that do not have a regional development program under this government.
Since January 1, 1989, when the so-called free trade agreement became law, 148,000 manufacturing jobs have been lost in Ontario alone. High interest rates, an artificially high Canadian dollar, rationalization and centralization of corporate business, have pulled industries out of small town Ontario and cities alike. Jobs have moved to Mexico, the U.S. and elsewhere. High taxes caused by 33 tax increases under this Tory government, high fuel costs and other transportation expenditures have driven jobs from Canada.
U.S. farmers are benefiting under free trade but Canadian farmers are not. Post offices, VIA Rail and potential tourist infrastructure have been taken away from the regions of Canada. Canadians want a lower Canadian dollar. They want tax relief, but most of all Canadians want a new government that knows what this Canadian nation is all about.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to bring to the attention of all members that this is Canadian Occupational Health and Safety Week. This is a week dedicated to highlighting the important role of health and safety programs that they have in the workplace in reducing the number of illnesses and the accidents that cost society so much each year.
At the federal level the Department of National Health and Welfare is responsible for the health and safety of all federal government employees. Health and Welfare Canada through its public service health programs provide a wide range of services to protect and to promote the mental, physical and social well-being of federal employees. Two of their current priorities are, increasing the capacity to respond to post-trauma stress and also a continuing emphasis on investigating complaints about the poor quality of air in the workplace.
The health and safety of our federal employees is important and I am confident their interests are being well served by this department.

Mr. Speaker, the International Festival of Lanaudiere will start its fourteenth season of activities this week. A marvellous program of classical music will be presented from June 20 to July 28. The audience will hear world famous performers, including new French singer Frangoise Pollet. Mozart will be in the spotlight on this 200th anniversary of his death, with a number of concerts by performers like Christopher Hogwood and the Handel and Haydn Society.
The festival's amphitheatre, in a breathtaring setting unique in this country, has room for 2,000 people under its roof and 8,000 more on the lawn, whose natural slope offers an excellent view of the stage. The visual impact, however, is nothing compared to the acoustics where no effort has been spared to render the subtle harmonies of our virtuoso performers as faithfully as possible.
This year, the festival will include the biggest hologram in the world, one of the few to be exhibited outside. It was made by artist Georges Diens who was inspired by the Champs Elysees in Paris.
I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but his time is expired.

Mr. Speaker, today we met with a group of individuals representing coal mining communities in western Canada. What they told us was both sad and shocking. It seems that for a number of reasons their industry is losing ground to competitors in the United States.
Western Canadian producers are subject to high transportation costs, including the GST, which American producers are not. If this government is serious about increasing interprovincial trade, it should look at a tax rebate for the transportation of goods from one province to another.

Also I would like to remind all members of the House that coal produced in western Canada is on balance cleaner and less damaging to the environment than the American product. It is time that this government showed support for western Canada coal producers, mine workers and the communities that depend on them.
I call upon the federal government to take immediate steps to remove the barriers from interprovincial trade.

Mr. Speaker, the 10th World Folklore Festival of Drummondville will be held from July 5 to July 14, and I invite all members and all Canadians to come and take part in the most important traditional event in Quebec.
For ten days, under the festival theme "Dix ans au rythme du monde", more than 30 folk dance groups from 21 countries will share with us their customs and traditions through music, dance and song, as well as a host of interesting activities. More than 800 performers from Canada, the United States, France, and countries as far away as the U.S.S.R., Poland and Argentina, will demonstrate their age-old, enchanting traditions through the medium of the dance.
About 1,300 volunteers have been working very hard for many months to make this popular festival a world class event. Last year, Mr. Speaker, the festival, which was named tourism event of the year, welcomed 750,000 visitors.

Mr. Speaker, it is ironic that U.S. authorities are attempting to restrict Canadian manufactured motor vehicles when the Canadian Department of Transport is proposing to relax the Motor Vehicle Safety Act to give preferred treatment to U.S. manufactured vehicles in Canada.
I find it puzzling and unacceptable that U.S. manufacturers will be allowed to supply a product in Canada that Canadian manufacturers are prevented by law to supply.
In my view, this move will dilute and confuse the Motor Vehicle Safety Act in Canada. It will increase the cost of new cars to consumers and it will transfer jobs to the United States.
It is unacceptable to have two sets of safety standards. It is imperative that the U.S. industry be required to meet the same standards as Canadian industry in Canada. The Department of Transport must review these amendments and assure the Canadian industry a level playing field in our own country.

Mr. Speaker, the war in the gulf may be over but the casualties continue to mount.
The UN Undersecretary-General referred to the near apocalyptic conditions following coalition bombing of Iraq. UNICEF has reported Iraqi children have stopped growing because they are not getting enough to eat. Waterborne diseases are widespread.
Surely Canada must urge the immediate lifting of non-military economic sanctions against Iraq. As the UN Secretary-General reported in March, the Iraqi people may soon face a further imminent catastrophe which could include epidemic and famine if life supporting needs are not rapidly met.
The Canadian Physicians for the Prevention of Nuclear War have asked: How is it possible that the
June 19, 1991

international community allowed its governments to place an entire civilian population in such jeopardy? Canada must accept our share of the responsibility for rebuilding after the carnage of this tragically wrong war.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Chilliwack is a very friendly and close community. So when part of the community comes under stress and strain, the community comes together in support of its neighbours.
There is stress and strain in Chilliwack right now because there are some vicious rumours that part of our community might come under attack. The Canadian Forces Base is an integral part of the community in Chilliwack, and many people are concerned that it might be closed.
This is causing a great many people in Chilliwack and throughout British Columbia serious concern. As I speak, the First Combat Engineer Regiment is in Kuwait clearing mines. The families are already stressed by the absence of their loved ones. It is encouraging to know that when times get rough and stress gets high, people pull together. Such is the case in Chilliwack where military families are supporting each other and where the community is rallying in support of the base.
I have confidence that the cabinet, when it deals with this, will let common sense prevail and that Chilliwack will remain a stronger, more cohesive community that is 100 per cent intact.

I know that hon. members would want to join me in welcoming our new parliamentary tour guides who will be introducing Parliament to visitors from Canada and around the world. They have been at work since May and will welcome over 300,000 people before the summer is over.

I am sure that all hon. members will want to join me in thanking the parliamentary pages whose terms will end shortly.

I am sure all members will agree that the young men and women who were selected to serve as pages have shown they are worthy representatives of Canadian youth, of whom we are justly proud.

You leave this Chamber with our very best wishes for your future. We hope to see some of you back in this Chamber, in a different role perhaps, in a few years.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
Every 17 minutes, there is a sexual assault committed in Canada. Ninety per cent of the victims are women. Women across this country, including women on all sides of this House, are afraid to walk in their own neighbourhoods at night.
In light of these tragic facts and in recognition of the Montreal massacre, will the Prime Minister today announce a royal commission to examine the tragedy of this war against women?

On the east coast, the Thompson case, an inmate committed a murder while on parole. There is concern in my community that he will receive a temporary absence to Moncton or be moved to a minimum security facility.
Is the minister satisfied with the way in which violent and sex offenders are receiving escorted temporary absences?

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. Just over a year and a half ago, all members of this House shared the tears of the parents of the victims of the Montreal massacre. Before and since then, many of us in this House have talked about violence against women.
The report of the subcommittee on the status of women, entitled War on Women has made some extremely useful recommendations, has heard a number of witnesses, men and women from across this country who came to speak to this committee and share the pain of violence. They asked this committee to do something, to
Oral Questions
take direct action. It is not only the victims, it is the abusers and it is the children who suffer from violence.
Does the Prime Minister accept the recommendations of the report by the subcommittee to really do something about violence against women or does he support the views of those on his side of the House who rejected this report and refused to endorse it?
My hon. friend, I think, does perhaps an injustice to some colleagues in the House of Commons. There has been no rejection of any of the provisions of the report.
Many refused to endorse it.

There has been no rejection. As I understand from the distinguished member from Calgary, there was a desire for an opportunity for members of the House to be seized of this and to debate it. There was no rejection.
They had it over a week.

My hon. friend is asking me an important question and I am trying to give an answer. I was not a member of the committee or of the subcommittee. All I know is that the member for Don Valley North, the chairperson of the committee, Barbara Greene, has done an outstanding job.
Hear, hear.

To the best of my knowledge, no one has voted against a single provision of the report. The object of the exercise is to bring the subcommittee report forward to the coiwnittee and eventually to have the House of Commons enact legislation pursuant to the recommendations of that report. That, I believe, is exactly what will happen.

Mr. Speaker, the women of Canada have waited a long time to see some serious work on the issue of violence against women. All of us in this House, I am sure, want to see that happen, but we want action now. When we want to put grain handlers back to work, we do it in a day. When want to ensure that arms sales can take place, this government does it in a day.
Will the Prime Minister endorse the recommendations of this subcommittee's report? Will he make sure that these come forward quickly for action now, for the women of Canada, for the children of Canada and end violence in this society, not just talk about it.

Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am advised that the committee has voted to table the report, which makes it a proper subject of public discussion and that it contains recommendations that touch a number of departments in government. But I think it is important to point out that the government continues now to be actively involved in seeking ways to deal with this problem concretely through legislative and policy initiatives.
As the hon. member will know, I just recently hosted in Vancouver an historic three-day meeting on Women, Law and the Administration of Justice which was historic because it involved high level presentation from the judiciary, representation from every Department of the Attorney General in this country, high level experts in the area of violence against women and other areas related to women and the law. This was a working group that was designed to conform with recommendations that we can act on.
We will look forward, with great interest, to the recommendations coming forward from the parliamentary committee, but we are working now on dealing with the issue of violence against women.

A supplementary, Mr. Speaker, for the Prime Minister.
Clearly, the women of Canada do not feel that. I think this is the issue. The issue is whether this government is prepared to seriously address the whole issue of violence against women.

This afternoon, Mr. Speaker, the provincial, territorial and federal ministers responsible for the Status of Women are meeting in St. John's, Newfoundland.
Which recommendations will the Minister responsible for the Status of Women announce at this meeting, those contained in the report or those rejected by her cabinet colleagues who refuse to acknowledge the tragedy of violence against women?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, because the committee, as I understand, voted to table its report, the meeting of Ministers responsible for the Status of Women will be free to discuss it. Mr. Speaker, yesterday in Montreal, Algo Group Inc., Canada's leading apparel manufacturer became the latest Canadian firm to announce its likely departure to the United States.
I would like to ask the Minister of Finance whether this is what he had in mind when he said to the OECD in Paris a couple of weeks ago: "Those who lose jobs during periods of economic slow-down such as we are now experiencing may well find their new positions in different industries, occupations or regions".
Why does the minister not have the courage to admit these effects of his policies at home? What industries, occupations and regions is he referring to and what policies is the government bringing in to help workers through these periods of adjustment?

Goose Bay has been an important northern base since 1942. It still serves our NATO allies and it is the main economic mainstay of the 8,000 people who live there. My question is how can the government contemplate closing Goose Bay when it has absolutely no defence policy for this country? Will the government give an

The United States and all of our allies are changing some important elements of their defence posture as a result of changes in the Soviet Union and eastern Europe. All NATO members are doing precisely that.
The German government has announced a reduction of some 180,000 troops in Germany alone. Canada will of course be examining options that will best serve our national interests while maintaining the integrity of a very highly skilled and professional military.

Canadian Forces Base Shilo is a first-class military base and the third largest employer in Manitoba with nearly 1,600 permanent military and civilian personnel, as well as hundreds of part-time and contract jobs.
How then could this government intend to close this first-class military base and still make sense in the absence of a comprehensive national defence policy? Will the minister make an undertaking today that he will first consult with Manitobans before considering any change in the status of CFB Shilo in Manitoba?

Mr. Speaker, the member for Portage-Interlake and the member for Brandon-Souris have both made repeated interventions on behalf of Manitoba in regard to this very excellent military installation. Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Statistics Canada today published a study which destroys the government's favourite argument that it is social program spending that is the cause of the country's deficit. The study shows that social spending has not increased relative to Gross Domestic Product for the last 16 years.
Will the Minister of Finance take this study seriously, this study which shows that it is corporate tax breaks and the high interest rate policies of successive Liberal and Conservative governments that are the main causes of the deficit? Will the minister take steps to end the generosity of his government to the corporate elite and to wealthy individuals in Canada and show that he is serious about the deficit?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. member will agree with me when I say that one of our biggest challenges in terms of cost pressures is the cost of servicing the national debt, the national debt we inherited from the Liberals when we took office in 1984.
Yes, this government has been generous toward social programs in this country and it continues to be. For the record, the last five years, in terms of major transfers to the provinces, which is largely for the purpose of sustaining health and education and other benefits that go to help the average Canadian, have increased from the last five-year period of $150 billion to $183 billion during this fiscal period.

Mr. Speaker, with respect, that is not what the study shows. The study shows that social spending has remained the same over the last 16 years. I grant the Minister of Finance that the deficit is in large part due to corporate tax breaks created by the Liberal Party of Canada. But that does not exempt this government from the fact that they have refused to
close many of the main loopholes that still exist from that time.
Will the Minister of Finance give a commitment in this House today, given that the Minister of National Health and Welfare is meeting with his counterparts today and tomorrow, that social spending in this country will not be asked to contribute one more cent to the elimination of the deficit, a deficit that social spending did not create. When will the corporate elite be asked to pay down the deficit?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I just indicated to the hon. member that for the five-year fiscal period ending 1991-92, the amount of federal transfers to the provinces amounted to $150 billion. Mr. Speaker, this government formed the Brander-Smith committee which examined this whole question. The Brander-Smith report that was tabled with the Ministry of Transport some months ago is a very, very comprehensive and very serious work. We have been examining the different components of it and are on the verge of making some recommendations and decisions as to what needs to be done to take into consideration the contents of the Brander-Smith report.

Mr. Speaker, my question today is for the Minister of Finance.
The Canadian dollar continues to climb in relation to the U.S. dollar. There have been many claims that this is because of a secret deal made between Canada and the U.S. as part of the free trade deal.
I was wondering if the minister could tell us today about the true value of the Canadian dollar and if indeed there is any relationship to the free trade agreement.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the exchange rate of the dollar has absolutely nothing to do with the free trade agreement. As the hon. member knows, we have a floating exchange rate. The value of the Canadian dollar is established in the marketplace based upon many factors, i.e. commodity prices, balance of payments, capital movements, inflation, inflationary pressures and interest rates. All of those components are part and parcel of the value of the dollar.
I think one of the reasons that the dollar is enjoying a high value is simply the fact that many foreigners are investing in Canada. It is a clear demonstration of the confidence that is being expressed in the Canadian economy.

Mr. Speaker, the minister has already given the indications of the government. We are very concerned about the situation in Cape Breton. It has been a tough time in Cape Breton for as long as I can remember, 30 or 40 years. Successive governments have wrestled, with varying degrees of success, with very serious structural problems in the economy in Cape Breton.
We began with Enterprise Cape Breton. We had some successes and, as the report indicated, some failures. The cost of attracting jobs to Cape Breton pursuant to some of the programs that the previous government initiated and we initiated was deemed by some outside observers to be excessively high.
ACOA, which Premier McKenna has described as the most important regional development agency ever introduced into Atlantic Canada, is contributing in some substantial way to some successes in Cape Breton, but we are cognizant of the problem that my hon. friend raises.
We are also aware that decade after decade we have failed as a country to successfully resolve some of these serious problems in Cape Breton. I give my hon. friend the undertaking that the Government of Canada in co-operation with the Government of Nova Scotia will try even harder to bring about a greater degree of prosperity and social justice throughout eastern Nova Scotia and into Cape Breton.

The hon. member knows very well how we got to the list. It was through great discipline in keeping just one member of the party up in opposition so there was only one person the Speaker could go to. Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I want to draw the attention of the House to a very important date, June 25, next Tuesday, because that is the anniversary for at least seven members of this House of Commons who were elected some 23 years ago on June 25,, 1968.
They include yourself, Mr. Deputy Chairman of Committees, and the Deputy Prime Minister. This illustrious group of members also includes the hon. member for Regina-Lumsden who is sitting down here and the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville who I guess is not in the House today, a very distinguished member. It includes also the hon. member for Davenport who sits right here but has just stepped out of the House, the hon. member for York Centre and myself.
Hear, hear.

I might mention that the hon. member for Papineau-Saint-Michel who was elected actually in a by-election in the fall of 1967 has been adopted by the class of 1968 as an integral part of our group.
I might say that 1968 was a really great year, and I think most of the members of the Official Opposition would agree with that. It was great for many reasons, but especially because we were just coming out of our country's centennial year and we showed great optimism, great hope and great confidence in our country.
As we go into this year, with all its trials, tribulations and great difficulties, I hope that we may find anew using those traditional Canadian feelings of of tolerance, goodwill and understanding the hope, the confidence and the optimism that we had in 1968 and go on to build a better and even stronger Canada.

June 19, 1991

I want to say also that the hon. member for York Centre is a second offender because he did not serve the whole time. He got knocked off in one election and came back again in the next one. speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the TVeasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I tabled yesterday in this House a bill setting out what is probably the most important Public Service reform plan in nearly a quarter of a century.
Economic conditions may command stringent wage constraints, but they must not stop us from having a broader vision. For Canada to be competitive on all fronts, changes have to be made now to produce, in time, a more modem and efficient Public Service.
Mr. Speaker, I rise before the House today to provide the honourable members with a statement on the status of collective bargaining in the Public Service. I believe it is important that Members are aware of the current situation and that the facts be clearly presented.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that in the February 26 Budget, the then Minister of Finance set out the government's wage policy for the next three fiscal years. In fiscal year 1991-92, salary budgets in departments are frozen at the level of the previous year.
The Minister indicated at the time that any negotiated wage increase this year would require a corresponding reduction in employment and that, in any case, the government would not contemplate wage increases this year of more than 3 per cent. In the following two fiscal years, provision is made for annual increases of up to 3 per cent.
This approach, Mr. Speaker, was imposed by economic necessity, balanced by a desire to continue collective bargaining with the unions. In that spirit, I met with the leaders of the Public Service unions on the day following the Budget to explain the Budget policy to them person-naly, and to seek their cooperation in negotiating agreements that the Canadian public can afford.

June 19, 1991
Routine Proceedings
Since February, there have been regular collective bargaining sessions with Public Service unions representing 58 of the 80 bargaining units and 184,000 of the
190,000	employees subject to collective agreements. I regret to inform the House that unions generally have not agreed to accept, in their negotiating demands, the limits established by the Budget-and the fiscal situation that lies behind it.
Union leaders have continued to make wage and benefits demands that are well beyond the capacity of the public purse. Indeed the leadership of the two largest unions, the Public Service Alliance of Canada and the Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada have, to my considerable regret, publicly stated that their unions will take whatever action is required to force the government to change its wage policy.

The government and the country are faced with a fiscal situation which must be addressed. The government outlined its full dimensions in the budget and we owe it to the Canadian public, who are faced with the corrosive effects of recession in every sector of the economy, to live within the measures announced at that time. The fiscal imperatives are clear. We must contain both the deficit and inflationary pressures if interest rates are to be brought down to a level that will lead to a sustained economic recovery.
Continued federal government leadership in dealing with inflationary public sector wage pressures is an essential part of this strategy. The actions of the six provinces which have followed our lead since the budget show that it is the right course.
As President of the Treasury Board I must pursue this objective in a way that preserves the integrity of government services to the Canadian public while minimizing the impact on public employees.
In addition, this government is engaged in a far-reaching process of renewal in the Public Service which I do not wish to see compromised. Its two cornerstones are a more service-oriented Public Service and greater attention to the human dimension in managing the Public Service.
My strong preference, therefore, is to continue to work with the unions to arrive at fair settlements for our employees which are within the limits of what the government and the taxpayers can afford to pay.
At the same time, I will be the first to acknowledge that the choices we have offered the unions are not very palatable to them any more than they are to the government. This is reflected in the current state of the collective bargaining negotiations.
By June 21, the last day before the summer recess of Parliament, 55 of the 80 bargaining units representing some 165,000 employees will have collective agreements that have expired. In five cases, they have been expired for more than one year.
By the time Parliament convenes in September, a further eight agreements will have expired. Also, by that time as many as 38 bargaining units and 170,000 Public Service employees could be in a legal position to strike. In addition, we expect binding awards to be handed down in early July for 18 occupational groups represented by the Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada.

Mr. Speaker these are the facts of the situation. I would now like to advise the House of the guiding principles that the government intends to follow during the summer months as this situation unfolds. We will continue to press for negotiated settlements for as long as the unions are willing to come to the table. We owe this much to our employees and to the system of collective bargaining itself, which has served both employer and employees well over the years.
But we will move swiftly and firmly if the situation deteriorates unacceptably. We will seek the recall of Parliament to enact the necessary legislation if there are illegal strikes or if there is unreasonable disruption in service to the public.
As announced in the Budget, we will act to modify any arbitral awards that go beyond the 0-3-3 guidelines to bring them in line with the Budget. If we are forced to introduce legislation, it will cover all departments and agencies for which the Treasury Board is the employer as well as other public bodies that are dependent to a significant degree on Parliamentary appropriations. This would include Parliament and its employees. And the same terms will aply to all: a 0 per cent increase in wages in fiscal year 1991-92 or in the period immediately following the expiry of a collective agreement and 3 per cent in the following year.
June 19, 1991

Three groups whose contracts had already been the subject of protracted negotiations before the Budget- the Translation, Auditing, and Computer Systems Administration groups-will be provided with higher settlements for the period before this fiscal year, but they too will then be covered by 0 and 3.
This legislation, then, would apply for the first two years of the three-year compensation restraint program announced in the February 26 Budget. The government remains committed to the Budget ceiling of 3 per cent in the third year of the program. The Minister of Finance announced in the Budget inflation targets for the next five years: 3 per cent by the end of 1992; 2 1/2 per cent by the middle of 1994; and 2 per cent by the end of 1995. These reduced inflation levels should allow us to achieve the third year of the compensation restraint program through collective bargaining.
Having stated my desire to continue to negotiate, I recognize that for some bargaining groups it may not be feasible to expect a voluntary agreement by the time the House returns on September 16. If this proves to be the case, I think it will probably be in the best interests of all concerned to introduce compensation restraint legislation at that time to cover those who have not been able to settle for at least a two-year agreement within the 0-3-3 limits. I am very conscious that this would mean the suspension of collective bargaining for this round, but it may be the fairest course to take under the circumstances.

These are hard measures, made necessary by hard times. In the economic climate in which we live, I do not think it is unreasonable to expect public sector employees to assume their share in working toward recovery. In my own recent travels across Canada, I met with Public Service employees at all levels and in all regions. I have concluded that these employees who, after all, are taxpayers themselves, are prepared to accept lower wage increases over the short term in order to make the future brighter for us all.
I received a second message both from union leaders and employees. The recession and the government's fiscal situation have created profound and, I do agree, understandable uncertainties in the minds of Public Service employees about the risks of losing their jobs. They are aware of the job losses and of the sacrifices that are being felt in the private sector and they are deeply conscious of the potential implications for themselves of
Routine Proceedings
the wage targets announced in the budget. This uncertainty also undermines the effective delivery of government services, and I want to put an end to it.
On May 29 I advised union leaders that the government had effectively lost any room it might have had to negotiate wage settlements for the current fiscal year at an increase of more than zero per cent. To proceed with a 3 per cent increase three months into the fiscal year would probably mean releasing more than the 6,000 employees forecast in the budget.
The other side of this coin is that a freeze on wage levels eliminates for all practical purposes the necessity to reduce further the number of jobs in the Public Service during the period of such a freeze. We will continue to need to change or eliminate specific jobs as the Public Service adjusts to changing demands for its services. Here and now I can make a commitment that every current employee of the Public Service who is affected by any such changes resulting from the budget will be offered a position on comparable terms for the period for which the wage freeze applies, if he or she is willing to be trained or relocated.
In that spirit I would also like to announce that departments will be instructed not to proceed with contingency plans which they were asked to develop at the time of the budget to absorb any wage increases in 1991-92 above zero per cent. There will, therefore, be no reason for lay-offs in the balance of this fiscal year as a consequence of the budget.
This is not job security in the sense in which unions negotiating demands too often mean it; a guarantee of lifetime employment. It is not this kind of job security. That would be unacceptable. Like good employers in the private sector, we recognize that it is in the interests of the employer and employees alike to have as much continuity and certainty as possible in order to have a productive and stable workforce.
This government's record in redeploying employees whose jobs are eliminated for other reasons is an excellent one, as the experience of the recently completed five-year downsiding program demonstrates. This has been thanks to the workforce adjustment policy which has provided an equitable safety net for employees. That policy expires on June 30 of this year. However, we are very much interested in negotiating a new one, in consultation with the unions under the auspices of the National Joint Council. In doing so we are prepared to explore ways of alleviating union concerns about the effects of contracting out in particular.

Routine Proceedings
Our discussions with union representatives have made good progress and I am hopeful that we can arrive at an agreement.

Mr. Speaker, today I am asking the leadership of the Public Service unions to go an extra mile with us in avoiding major disruption to the Canadian public this summer.
In my time as President of the Treasury Board, I have developed a great respect for them personally and for the system of collective bargaining that is one of the foundations of our Public Service. I know they share the priority that I give to maintaining the highest possible quality of service to the Canadian public.
I know too that the union leaders understand that the government will not deviate from the terms of the February 26 Budget, especially at a time when there is mounting evidence that we are on the right track and have the strong backing of Canadians for what we are seeking to do.
But I believe there continues to be real scope within the Budget to arrive at negotiated settlements that meet the needs of our employees. The government will introduce legislation if it must, but I would prefer to try to make the established insitutions of staff relations work in these difficult times as well as they do in better circumstances.

Mr. Speaker, in 1984 this government was elected on the illusory promises of fiscal responsibility, solving the economic problems of the country and jobs, jobs, jobs. Seven years later 1.5 million Canadians are unemployed, the debt and the interest it is costing have more than doubled, and the nation has been in an unnecessary, made-in-Ca-nada recession created by this government. Canadians have been realizing for some time that the Emperor has no clothes, no vision and certainly no economic plan.
Today's statement is the culmination of the government's abject failure to meet its commitment to Canadians, to provide them with good government with quality services at an affordable price.
The statement today appears, like so much the government has done, on an ad hoc basis, decided at the last minute, thrown before Parliament without adequate forethought. In fact, as the person expected to reply to this motion, I heard that from the press that this statement would be made, not from the minister's office.
Yesterday, the President of the Treasury Board presented a package of so-called reform and revitalization of the Public Service. I must remind the minister and Canadians that this has been the foremost Public Service in the world, up until recently.
He said that this bill would help Public Service employees to concentrate on service to citizens rather than serving systems. He added that Canadians expect a Public Service that is effective and up to date, which is staffed and led by Canada's ablest men and women.
In this statement today the same minister has shown that he has no understanding of how to build commitment, competence and progressive thinking and service to the public in the Public Service of Canada.
I marvel at the minister's audacity to stand up again, in a final display of disregard, on the eve of the recess of Parliament. It is a display of disregard for workers' rights, threatening to call Parliament back, threatening to introduce legislation when he cannot negotiate a zero increase this year, even threatening to override the decisions of impartial third party adjudicators.
The minister says he has a desire to continue collective bargaining, an admirable statement. The minister should bargain with the unions at the table, and not on the floor of the House of Commons.
May I interject on a point of order? I am finding it increasingly difficult to speak with the rabble going on around me.
June 19, 1991

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order, please. The Speaker finds it difficult to speak with some of the static that is going on over at that side of the House.
I would just hope you would keep it down, please.

Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. There is a lobby outside and if people want to be disruptive, they can do it there.
The minister quotes economic necessity as the reason for this statement today and for the regressive and excessive measures announced in the February 26 budget. The economic necessity has been created by this government, not by the workers, not by the employees. The economic necessity arises directly from this government's policies: high interest rates, a high dollar which is hurting our manufacturers and hurting our exports, high unemployment and unprecedented tax increases.
The recession has been created by this government, not by Canadian workers. Particularly, federal public sector workers have shown remarkable restraint in wage demands, giving a complete lie to the minister's statement that the unions representing Public Service employees have been irresponsible in their wage demands.
The minister calls on the public sector workers to assume their share in working toward recovery. That is exactly what they have done. The minister knows perfectly well that federal government workers have led the way for over half a dozen years, in wage restraint, accepting wage settlements below the rate of inflation, accepting wage settlements below those of any other public sector worker and accepting wage settlements far below those of the private sector.
He gets up today and pretends to the Canadian public that somehow federal public sector workers have been driving inflation and driving economic problems, and that is simply not an accurate reflection of reality. It is a reflection of the fact that the government wants to try and pretend that somehow it is those who work for the people of Canada who are responsible for the fiscal and economic problems this government has created.
The government served a signal on February 26 that it had no intention of bargaining in good faith. I want to say very clearly in this House that the Liberal Party introduced collective bargaining into the Public Service of Canada and the Liberal Party will continue to defend collective bargaining in the Public Service of Canada.
The government has stalled on negotiations. It calls on the unions in this statement to come back to the table. It
Routine Proceedings
is the government that has stalled on negotiations and has not been negotiating. It is not negotiation when you sit down at the table and say "this is what you are going to get." The minister's concept of negotiation is like the concept of justice in some countries: "Yes, we will give you an open, public trial. Yes, you can call witnesses, but in the end you are going to get executed." That is not justice and this is not collective bargaining.
Unions have not accepted the bargaining by blackmail which this government tried to introduce by saying very clearly to people at the beginning of the process, before they had any discussions or any negotiations, here is the bottom line, like it or lump it, and the bottom line was this: you can either get a fair salary increase this year or you can sacrifice the jobs of your fellow employees.
The unions, I think quite properly, have said they are not prepared to bargain away the jobs of their fellow workers. This kind of bargaining by blackmail simply is not the way we operate in a democratic nation. We operate in a democratic nation by workers, employees and their employer sitting down and trying to reach a reasonable solution.
Since February 26, this government has precluded that happening. It has given employees every reason, in this statement today, to know that it is not dealing in good faith with its employees. They know that. They have those cases before the courts and those cases will be dealt with before the courts.
But clearly, when you sit down at a bargaining table and say this is going to be the end result, no negotiations take place, no negotiations have taken place and no negotiations can take place. For the minister to try and blame the employees for the outcome of that kind of bargaining by blackmail, is simply not a fair representation to Canadians or to this House of the situation.
The minister has said that the fiscal situation is responsible for this. Well this government has created the fiscal situation.
I ask Canadians, as I ask all members of Parliament, to listen to the messages we have had from this government. For six consecutive budgets it said: "We have a debt problem. We have a deficit problem. Here are tough measures to deal with the debt and deficit. We are asking all Canadians to pay more, to get less, to do with less, tighten their belt buckles so we can get rid of the debt and the deficit." That is six consecutive years of promises to do something about the debt and the deficit and it keeps going up.

June 19, 1991
Routine Proceedings
Canadians are starting to wonder if this government has any idea what it wants to do about the debt and the deficit because every single solution it has proposed has failed to work.
No credibility. No trust.

This government claims fiscal responsibility. I sat in meetings of the public accounts committee where Treasury Board officials said: "We cannot tell you if you are saving money by your downsizing program because we cannot tell you what you are spending on contracting out or short-term employees".
In other words, while contracting out has gone up by billions of dollars, while the Public Service of Canada has been destabilized, while service to the old, the young and the sick has been suffering, this government is totally unconcerned about how much money it is wasting on contracting out. In fact, for all the Canadian public knows, for all the public accounts committee knows, for all this House knows, we are spending twice as much on services, through contracting, as we were six or seven years ago, because this government simply does not know. Is that fiscal responsibility? Of course it is not.
The government will cite its commitment to austerity in the bill that says: "Well members of Parliament are going to restrain their own wages in line with the restraint on public sector wages." We note that the government did not decide to restrain its own wages based on this year's collective bargaining when public servants' wages are to be frozen. Oh, no, we, as members of Parliament, are not going to put ourselves in that boat. We are waiting until next year when we are promising the Public Service 3 per cent.
That kind of hypocrisy is something of which Canadians are sick and tired. That kind of hypocrisy is something that makes it impossible for public servants to work with confidence and with trust in partnership with this government.
Who is really going to suffer? It is easy when you are earning over $100,000 a year to say: "Oh well, I will do without a salary increase this year", or "I will accept 3 per cent next year". Who is going to really suffer? How
about those tens of thousands of people, 80 per cent of them women, who are earning under $19,000 a year? They are the ones who are going to suffer. Is there any special provision for them?
How about the 68,000, nearly one-third of public sector employees, who earn incomes below the poverty line?
That is not the message that this government wants to get out there. It wants to get out the message that everybody working for the federal government is a fat cat, living high off the hog, working maybe one-quarter of the day. They know that it is not true and they have a duty to tell the public of Canada that it is not true.
The minister promises no further job cuts. Does he think anybody believes that? My phone has been ringing for months with calls from people. We are cutting out things like health promotion services and people are losing their jobs. We are cutting out or eliminating supervision of drug residues in foods in Health and Welfare and it is probably still going on today.
People are losing their jobs and Canadians are losing valuable services.
A few years ago we had a five-year downsizing program which is now finished. It ended at the end of last year. Now we have another downsizing program. The minister has said that they told departments not to implement their downsizing. That is not very believable when today in government departments across the country people are being told they do not have jobs and are on surplus.
If you were going to cut the fat in government you might look at the most bloated cabinet in any nation in the free world. You might want to look at why cabinet ministers have doubled the number of employees they can take out of those over-worked government offices and put to their own personal and political service. They have doubled the number that they can use, doubled the costs to the Canadian public, and cut services to Canadians.
June 19, 1991

Perhaps we on this side of the House should be happy that 1.3 million people who work for the public sector across Canada are seeing this government for what it is because they are not going to want to vote for it, they and all their families, friends and neighbours. Perhaps we should be happy about that. We are not. We are not because we know it will be Canadians who suffer.
Seventy per cent of the Public Service is not here in the national capital region, not at the beck and call of members of Parliament and members of cabinet. Seventy per cent is out there across the country in communities from the 12,000 in Victoria, to the 18,000 in Halifax, to the 9,000 in Newfoundland, delivering service to Canadians. Cutbacks are hurting Canadians. We saw with the ships' crews it is rescues at sea that suffer when public servants are not there to do the job. Seniors suffer when they cannot even get a simple answer to a pension request for over six weeks. The unemployed suffer when they are trying to feed a family when they are out of a job and the unemployment office is so over-worked that there is going to be a six to eight week delay in the delivery of their cheques.
Canadians suffer when customs at the border are understaffed. Those who collect 25 per cent of the revenue that comes into the country are only collecting 40 per cent of what they could because they do not have enough people to do'the job.
We heard very recently in this House about cutbacks to health services to Canadians at a time when our medicare system is in desperate trouble because of the cutbacks of this government to the funding of medical services.
All those services which Canadians consider part of being Canadian, part of a just and compassionate society, part of a society which serves its people from coast to coast to coast are in danger because of the actions of this government.
This statement is a travesty. It has nothing to do with good management. It has nothing to do with good government. It has a lot to do with the politics of Preston Manning and the Reform Party. If Canadians wanted to see a precedent of what they are in for with the next Conservative government, or with a Preston Manning government, just let them watch. I ask Canadians this summer when some of their services may be disrupted to remember it is not the over-worked public servant behind the counter who is to blame, it is this government.
Routine Proceedings

Mr. Speaker, I share the views of the hon. member from the Liberal Party when I say how frustrating it is to have the opportunity to respond to a statement not even knowing that the minister is going to make a statement in the House.
On a day when we should be celebrating the end of a parliamentary session and heading home to our ridings and families, we face instead a day of mourning. After hearing the minister speak I think we have to acknowledge that we have heard the minister sound a death knell for collective bargaining in the public sector.
The minister in his speech said that on the day following the budget he met with the unions personally to seek their co-operation in negotiating agreements that the Canadian public could afford. The day after the budget he decided to consult, the day after the hammer came down the minister decided to consult. Not before the budget, not in any way being serious about consultation when that consultation was taking place after the fact.
The minister went on to say that the unions generally have not agreed to accept in their negotiating demands the limits established by the budget. What a surprise. They were consulted after the fact.
He went on to say that the leadership of the two largest unions, the Public Service Alliance of Canada and the Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada, have, to his regret, publicly stated that then-unions will take whatever action is required to force the government to change its wage policy.
That is exactly as it should be, because those union leaders were speaking on behalf of their membership after having had a free vote within their unions about what they thought about the government's policies.
Government after government, both Liberal and Conservative, have refused to legislate full free collective bargaining for public sector workers. Both those governments have treated their workers with great disdain; both have consistently refused to treat the men and women who work for them as partners. They have continued consistently, both governments, to treat them as adversaries.

June 19, 1991
Routine Proceedings
They cannot negotiate classification or pensions and there are a whole number of prohibited areas under the Public Service Staff Relations Act which the unions cannot negotiate. That act was passed 25 years ago. We have had a successive parade of Liberal and Tory governments ever since, for at least 20 of those 25 years, which have wanted to amend this legislation.
The government introduced Public Service 2000. Many of the attitudes at the bargaining tables and the reason many of the components have not completed their bargaining is because the government has been stalling, waiting for this legislation. Now we find out that the government introduces legislation which does not bring Public Service 2000 into a mode to be ready to go into the 21st century. As my colleague from Nickel Belt says, we should be calling this PS 1000 because you have taken us back to the dark ages.
The minister referred to continued federal government leadership in dealing with inflationary public sector wage pressures as an essential part of his strategy; "and the actions of six provinces which have followed our lead since the budget show that it is the right course". Everybody in this House knows and Canadians all across the country know that the Minister of Finance called together the finance ministers, cut a deal, and agreed before the federal budget came in that they would attack the public sector workers from coast to coast to coast in this country. The two governments in this country which have made it absolutely clear that they will live up to their collective agreements have been the Bob Rae government in Ontario and the Tony Penikett NDP government in the Yukon.
The fact that six other governments in this country have followed suit with this misguided Tory government does not mean that this government is following the right course. It means that six other Liberal and Tory governments are on the wrong course.
I would like to go on through the minister's comments.
He talks about a renewal of the Public Service which he does not wish to see compromised. Does he mean renewal with a hammer?
He talks about bringing the human dimension into managing the Public Service. The human dimension is back to work legislation. He is saying: "If you do not settle, we will tell you what you get". Is that the human dimension that the minister is speaking about? If that is the human dimension that this government talks about then I am surprised that this government has not introduced legislation to abolish collective bargaining in the public sector.
That is in fact what the minister is doing. He is calling it another name. He is saying: "If the unions do not settle by September 16, it does not matter that they are in a free collective bargaining process". If they do not settle, the minister has said: "We will tell you what you get. We will suspend collective bargaining for this round".
I wonder about a minister who says he is concerned about the human dimension in managing the public sector in one paragraph and in the next paragraph talks about suspending collective bargaining in this round.
He goes on to say that 55 of the 80 bargaining units representing some 165,000 employees as of tomorrow will have collective agreements that have expired, in five cases for more than a year.
It is interesting that when this government wants to make progress and wants things to happen-my leader mentioned during Question Period that it wanted the grain handlers' industry back in operation, it wanted gun sales legislation to go through-anything can be done by this government. When it comes to collective bargaining, this government has set the pace for the country for stall tactics.
Fifty-five out of 80 bargaining units are living with expired collective agreements. Yet, the minister says that if they do not settle by September 16 he will tell them what they get. He goes on to say that by that timemeaning September-as many as 38 bargaining units and
170,000	Public Service employees will be in a legal position to strike.
"Legal" is the operative word here. The minister very clearly stated today that "legal" means nothing. The minister has said that he will recall Parliament immediately to legislate these workers back to work whether the strike is legal or illegal. If they do not have a collective agreement by September he will tell them what they are going to get.
June 19, 1991

Free collective bargaining is something we should be very proud of in this House. He says he will continue to press for negotiated settlements for as long as the unions are willing to come to the table. When somebody announces to me that the deal is zero-three-three, that we are not moving on anything and that we are going to sit around and wait until the minister introduces the legislation.
He is going to draw up the legislation. We are going to adjourn for a couple of months and if the unions wait long enough we will tell them what they are going to get. Who the heck would want to come to the bargaining table? I am surprised that the unions have stayed at the table as long as they have.
He says: "We will seek the recall of Parliament to enact the necessary legislation if there are illegal strikes or unreasonable disruption of service". Again, "legal" does not mean anything. What is the point of having the right to legally strike in the public sector if the minute you do you are legislated back to work? That is a farce.
The minister talked about recognizing that for some bargaining groups it might not be feasible to expect a voluntary agreement by the time the House returns. It might not be feasible. Mr. Minister you said that. Yet, the minister is saying that he will introduce compensation restraint legislation at that time to cover those who have not been able to settle their agreement.
What is the point? The Treasury Board has no reason to bargain now. The union could keep coming to the table all summer long, but there is no reason to bargain. The minister has promised the Treasury Board bargainers: "Just hang out, guys, because on September 16 I am going to introduce legislation and you do not have to do the work you set out to do. I will do it for you". That is free collective bargaining, public sector style, under this government.
He says that on September 16 he will suspend collective bargaining for this round, but it may be the fairest course to take under the circumstances.
Why does he not just save time? Why does he not just introduce legislation today saying: "You have no rights, public sector workers. I am going to do it for you. I am going to tell you what you get". There is nothing fair about even one thing the minister said in his statement today. Not one thing he said was fair. Yet he says it may be the fairest course.
Routine Proceedings
He has concluded that these employees, after speaking to a number of public sector workers across the country, are prepared to accept lower wage increases over the short term in order to make the future brighter for us all.
I ask the minister to name names. I would like to know if any of those workers who were willing to take a lower wage to make life rosy for us all, were the women who are working at the poverty level for the federal Public Service.
I would like to know if any of those people he spoke to were women who were waiting for the promised pay equity under this federal government. I would like to know and I am anxiously going to await a response at some time from the minister on that count.
He says that the uncertainty undermines the effective delivery of government services and he wants to put an end to it. I guess it is better to be certain you are being beaten up by this government than to continue to be uncertain whether you are going to be beaten up by this government.
He says that for the period of the wage freeze he is willing to ensure that nobody is laid off if the union accepts the zero, three and three, and if workers are willing to be trained and relocated.
Just yesterday, in the briefing for PS 1000 the minister's representative told us-PS 1000, we are back to the dark ages here-that deployment or redeployment of public sector workers, in other words, moving them around, would be strictly voluntary. It would not be compulsory. Yet we have the minister saying today: "They will not be laid off if they are willing to be trained and relocated. No choice, just move".
The minister went on to refer to the work force adjustment policy, the fact that it has already expired and a new one will be developed in consultation with the unions. I have already spoken about the kind of consultation the public sector unions can expect from this government.
He says that our discussions with union representatives in the area of contracting out have made good progress, and he is hopeful that they will arrive at agreement. I challenge the minister to give an example of one government jurisdiction in this country where public sector contracting out has proven cheaper or more cost effective. In fact, yesterday the minister spoke of bringing the federal government more into line with the private sector.

June 19, 1991
Routine Proceedings
There are many people on the government side of the House who know that the private sector would not put up with the inefficiencies in the area of contracting out. The reason it would not is because it is not efficient, it is not productive, and it is not good for morale.
The minister has yet to show any of us one area where privatization or contracting out has been efficient or effective.
In fact Mr. Kenneth Dye, former Auditor General, referred to contracting out as "the government's greatest boondoggle". There have been studies done in British Columbia that outline very clearly how expensive contracting out becomes for government. Yes, you get rid of a few workers on your payroll, but you are paying out this big contract and you have to develop a whole new bureaucracy to supervise and look after the contracts.
It is very interesting that nobody has been able to show us how contracting out is effective.
The minister said that he would like to see the unions go the extra mile with the government to avoid disruption of the Canadian public this summer. Some 55 of 80 bargaining units representing 165,000 workers have had their collective agreements expire, five of those bargaining units for over a year, and the minister says: "I would like to see the unions go the extra mile".
I would like to see this government go even a few centimetres toward finding a solution to the collective bargaining process.
The minister said that he has developed a great respect for the workers personally and for the system of collective bargaining. What the minister said today does not indicate great or little respect for the collective bargaining process. In fact, it is questionable whether this minister has any respect at all for the collective bargaining process.
The minister really said it all when he said in his closing remarks that "the government will introduce
legislation if it must, but it would prefer to try to make the established institutions of staff relations work in these difficult times as well as they do in better circumstances".
He makes a farce of the free collective bargaining process and of arbitration by making that statement. If the government wants to run the government like the private sector, he had better start by treating the workers with respect. Instead of threatening back to work legislation and suspension of bargaining, he should introduce legislation providing for full free collective bargaining in all areas, as in the private sector. Then we would know that he is serious and then we could expect efficiency, enthusiasm and respect for this Parliament, this government and this employer from public sector workers.
