That, in accordance with subsection 49(1) of An Act respecting the status and use of the Official Languages of Canada, Revised statutes of Canada, Chapter 31 (4th Supplement), this House approves the appointment of Dr. Victor Goldbloom, as commissioner of Official Languages for Canada;
-He said: Mr. Speaker, first of all, speaking on behalf of the government, I would like to thank the former Commissioner of Official Languages, Mr. D'Iberville Fortier, for his dedication to the task at hand and for exceptional services rendered to the government in the course of a brilliant career that spanned four decades.

June 19, 1991
Routine Proceedings

Mr. Fortier first joined the public service in 1952 and served in Canada in diplomatic posts world-wide until his appointment as Commissioner of Official Languages nearly seven years ago. We extend our best wishes for the years to come.
It is a great pleasure for me to address the appointment of Dr. Victor Goldbloom as the next Commissioner of Official Languages. Knowing Dr. Goldbloom as I do, it came as no surprise to me that when the Prime Minister spoke with opposition leaders, both fully endorsed and welcomed the proposal and then approved it.

In fact, Dr. Goldbloom's background and his expertise in so many areas make him eminently suited to taking on the duties of Commissioner. He chaired the language rights committee of the Court Challenges Program. He is a native of Montreal and a graduate of McGill University. He practised as pediatrician and taught pediatrics for many years before entering public life.
He became chairman of the medical economics committee and was, successively, president of the Association des pediatres de la Province de Quebec, the Association medicale du Quebec and the Canadian Medical Association. In this latter capacity, he travelled across Canada, becoming acquainted with the health care systems and social problems of the provinces and territories.
In 1966, he was elected in the new riding of D'Arcy McGee as its first representative. He represented the riding in the National Assembly for nearly 14 years. In 1970 he was appointed minister and became the first member of the Jewish community to sit in the Quebec cabinet. Subsequently, he became Quebec's first Minister of the Environment.
In February 1973, he took over the Municipal Affairs portfolio, and in 1975, he also became the minister responsible for the Olympic Games facilities. Re-elected for a fourth term on November 15, 1976, he resigned his seat in the fall of 1979 to become president of the Canadian Council of Christians and Jews. From 1982 to 1990, he was president of the International Council of Christians and Jews.
Dr. Goldbloom has been the executive director of the Folds de la recherche en sante du Quebec since January 1990. The new commissioner is active in community life and participates in numerous voluntary associations: the Canadian Council for Native Business, the Jean Lesage Foundation, the Jewish Public Establishment Co-ordinating Committee, the Canadian Medical Association Subcommittee on Environmental Occupational Health, and chairs a task force for the Canadian Paediatric Society on Environmental Aspects of Day Care. He is a member of the board of the Quebec Drama Federation. He is an honorary patron of the Quebec Bar Association Foundation. Many of his accomplishments have been recognized. He is an honorary Doctor of Law at the University of Toronto, an Officer of the Order of Canada. He has received the Government of Canada Award for Race Relations and he is an officer of VOrdre nationale d Quebec.
In 1988 the government adopted a new Official Languages Act, which built on and improved the previous legislation. Dr. Goldbloom will have the critical responsibility of overseeing the realization of these provisions.
The role of the commissioner is an important one. He is an ombudsman, a servant of Parliament responsible for ensuring the recognition of both official languages and the compliance with the Official Languages Act by federal institution.

Mr. Goldbloom comes to this position at a critical time in our country's history. Our new Commissioner of Official Languages will undoubtedly want to take an active part in defining our country's identity, as did his predecessors.
Mr. Speaker, we-the government and I-are confident that Dr. Goldbloom will be successful on this important mission and we wish him the best of luck.

maintopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SUBCOMMITTEE
subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER OF OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my party, I am pleased to support the appointment of Dr. Victor Goldbloom as the Official Languages Commissioner for Canada. Dr. Goldbloom is the first anglophone Quebecer to fill this position. He is a bilingual Montrealer and a graduate of McGill University. All of these things we have in common with him. I

June 19, 1991

might also say that for 14 years he represented the provincial constituency of D'Arcy McGee, which shares territory with my federal constituency of Notre-Dame-de-Grace.
The hon. minister pointed out many of Dr. Gold-bloom's accomplishments, including the fact that he was president of both the Quebec Medical Association and the Canadian Medical Association. As minister, he was Minister of Municipal Affairs and the first Minister for the Environment in Quebec. Recently, he has been the president of the Canadian Council of Christians and Jews. Also he was president of the committee which decided whether or not certain individuals and groups should get funding to contest violations of their official language rights before the courts.
Mr. Goldbloom himself is from a minority in Canada. Consequently, I believe he will be extremely sensitive to the position of the linguistic minority communities in this country.
That having been said and without any criticism of the individual who is appointed-and we support that appointment-I must say that the process by which the government went about this appointment was deplorable and once again shows the great incompetency of the government.
The government knew more than one year ago that Mr. Fortier, the previous commissioner, was to resign on June 14, yet even last week it had not started consultations with the opposition parties on an appointment.
I want to point out that the Commissioner for Official Languages is an officer of Parliament. He is not an officer of the government. He reports to Parliament. He does not report to the government. Therefore, he requires the support of all political parties in this House. Consequently, it is incumbent on the government to consult closely, in advance, with the opposition parties. It did not do that. Mr. Fortier retired from his position last week and consultations only started this week, the week in which Parliament is to adjourn.
That having been said, I hope this statement on the record will assure that the next time in seven years' time-and this will not be forgotten-this will be done in a more proper manner and that the consultations will be done as I think they were intended.
Routine Proceedings
At the retirement party reception for Mr. Fortier, I congratulated Mr. Fortier and especially congratulated him for his close contact and communication with members of the Standing Committee on Official Languages. He was always in touch with us and he was always available. I also pointed out that he always acted with great balance and fairness and also with courage. If an ombudsman or a Commissioner for Official Languages is to be successful, he must be fair to all language communities in Canada and when he sees a violation of their language rights, he speaks out with courage and with forthrightness. That is what Mr. Fortier did and we are sure that Mr. Goldbloom will do the same.
Among the outstanding issues that Dr. Goldbloom will have to deal with, of course, is the fact that despite we passed the Official Languages Act in 1988, we still have not got in force the regulations that go with that Official Languages Act.
The government has presented to us draft regulations for service to the public. Those have been examined by the standing committee and referred back to the minister. One hopes that they will soon be in operation. But the government still has not provided us with the draft regulations relating to the language of work in the federal government or to equitable participation by English and French speaking Canadians in the Public Service of Canada. We are still waiting for that.
The former commissioner, Mr. Fortier, spoke out strongly demanding those regulations time and again.
The new commissioner will also have to deal with the attempt by certain groups in Canada to dilute and to step backward with respect to our policy on official languages. There are even rumours today that the Spicer commission next week will recommend a weakening of the commitment to official languages or a stepping back with respect to that policy.
I must remind the House, Mr. Speaker, through you, that this attempt-and this was even discussed at a behind the doors conference of the government-to move to a sort of Swiss model in Canada is totally out of context and ridiculous for Canada where we have a million francophones living outside of Quebec, more francophones living outside of Quebec than there were francophones altogether in 1867 at the time of Confederation, and 700,000 to 800,000 anglophones living in Quebec.

June 19, 1991
Routine Proceedings
So that model that is being suggested that Quebec would live entirely in French or work in French and the rest of Canada entirely in English is not to be accepted. One would hope that our new commissioner will deal as strongly with that as well.
The final issue is the attempt by the government by privatizing Crown corporations to the private sector and removing them from the ambit of the Official Languages Act. We were dealing with a bill that was before this House recently, making the point that in privatizing the airports in Canada they should not be exempt from all the provisions of the Official Languages Act. When Air Canada was privatized, it was privatized with all the obligations of the Official Languages Act imposed on it. We again have to be vigilant and the new commissioner will have to be vigilant to see that the government does not try to get away with those sorts of things.
Those are the difficult issues that the commissioner will have to deal with. We congratulate him on his appointment. We are here to support him. We are here to work with him and we know he will do a good job.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased today to congratulate the Prime Minister for having been able to convince Victor Goldbloom, an excellent choice, to accept the position of Commissioner of Official Languages. I would also like to congratulate Mr. Goldbloom, and to express my sympathy, to him, for he is taking on a demanding and difficult task. It is a difficult task because the expectations are very high. Many Canadians ask themselves questions about bilingualism. Is it a program that costs too much money? How much does it cost? Why all that money? Does bilingualism mean that a linguistic group has a better chance of obtaining a job in the federal public service? Those of us in this House that support bilingualism and the Official Languages Act know that there are good answers to those questions.
It is the job of the Commissioner of Official Languages to go out and talk with Canadians, to explain to them the importance of bilingualism, and to answer their questions about that very important act. However, Mr. Speaker, progress in the federal public service has been slow and inconsistent as regards bilingualism.
June 19, 1991

Routine Proceedings
For instance, I worked for months with a group of francophone members of the RCMP who did not get the bilingualism bonus, even after having won a very clear decision by the Federal Court. Those people are entitled to that bonus.
The Commissioner of Official Languages is the watchdog of the federal public service. His mandate is to ensure that the Act is implemented. I hope that Mr. Goldbloom can bark and has sharp teeth, because he will need those requirements.
The tensions between the different linguistic groups in that country are very strong and the francophone minorities are still fighting for their rights. The role of the Commissioner is essential to help this country find a common ground concerning those issues. Mr. Gold-bloom, an anglophone from Quebec, was a minister in the Quebec provincial government during a turbulent period. Therefore, he is well prepared to help find a solution to problems that he knows very well.
As for me, I would like to give three pieces of advice to our new Commissioner: First, to ensure the implementation of the Official Languages Act while always respecting the jurisdiction of the province of Quebec; secondly, to continue to build bridges between our two linguistic groups, by showing great patience and humility; and, thirdly, to oppose the efforts of this government which is trying to back off as regards the implementation of this essential piece of legislation. In other words: Don't give up!
I wish the best of luck to Mr. Goldbloom in his job as Commissioner of Official Languages, and I offer him all the assistance and cooperation that my party and I can provide, so that he can succeed in bridging the numerous gaps that still exists between our two linguistic groups.

maintopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SUBCOMMITTEE
subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER OF OFFICIAL LANGUAGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to welcome the new Commissioner for Official Languages, Mr. Victor Goldbloom.
Under the Official Languages Act, the duties and functions of the commissioner are defined as follows:
It is the duty of the Commissioner to take all actions and measures within the authority of the Commissioner with a view to ensuring recognition of the status of each of the official languages and compliance with the spirit and intent of this Act in the administration of the affairs of federal institutions, including any of their activities relating to the advancement of English and French in Canadian society.
Mr. Speaker, Mr. Goldbloom's predecessor carried out its duties with efficiency, vigour and a lot of courage. Indeed, always mindful of the mission this House gave him, Mr. D'Iberville Fortier had the courage to enforce the Official Languages Act, for which criticisms were sometimes levelled at him. He was able to honour his responsibilities and also the confidence placed in him by the linguistic communities. He showed the way for Mr. Goldbloom who now takes over.
Not only will Dr Goldbloom fill the shoes few people would fight over, but he will also have to sell the linguistic duality. Our new commissioner will have to say no to all those who would want to trade the official languages for the so-called sake of national unity. As the watchdog for the rights of linguistic minorities, that is of French-speaking Canadians outside Quebec as well as English-speaking Canadians inside Quebec, as the advocate of linguistic equality in our country, and on behalf of the minority he has the duty to protect, he will have to say "no".
Mr. Speaker, our new commissioner will have to continue to uphold these principles. He will have to explain to all Canadians the difference between institutional bilingualism and individual bilingualism. Several individuals who are against the Official Languages Act think this legislation aims at making Canada a bilingual country. Several people think that, under this legislation, all Canadians must become bilingual. And yet, this Act only ensures that all Canadians, whether they speak English or French, can be served in the official language of their choice in federal institutions. Why would anyone object to an English-speaking Quebecer being served in English by his or her government or a French-speaking Ontarian being served in French, when dealing for example with old age pensions or immigration or defence? Why would anyone be against an unemployed anglophone from Sherbrooke or an unemployed francophone from Vanier being given services or directions in his or her language?
The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms guarantees language minorities the right to education or trial in their own language. How can we logically transfer to the provinces the responsibility of enforcing those rights, when the majority in these provinces is not even abiding by them, Mr. Speaker.

June 19, 1991
Routine Proceedings
The message from the Federation des communautes francophones et acadiennes du Canada, last weekend, and the one from Alliance Quebec are very clear. Minorities do not intend to relinquish their rights and are planning to be very active during the constitutional debate. Minorities do not want to be left out and are planning to make themselves heard loud and clear. The new Commissioner will have to do the same.
Racists of all stripes are spreading lies and inflating the cost of bilingualism, hoping to fool the innocents. The present attacks come mostly from these defeatist groups which have never accepted the Canadian reality.
When we talk about official languages, we are talking of the co-existence of these two languages in Canada, and sometimes in some provinces or some parts of the country. We must stop blaming all the problems of Confederation on this co-existence. We must stop making it the scapegoat for all our problems. As some would say in my riding, Mr. Speaker, we must stop using bilingualism as the national ketchup to put on all the problems this country has.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, we must stop talking about the cost of language duality and start talking about its benefits.
Whether it is bilingualism, multiculturalism, native programs, fisheries, defence, the CBC, transportation or anything else, we must not see only the cost, especially if it is inflated, we must also judge the value. The only way to maintain Canadian unity is to keep the values which are the essence of this country.
The new Commissioner, Dr. Goldbloom, must face quite a challenge, but a challenge vital to the future of our country.
I wish him all the best in the fullfilling of his mandate. We would like to assure him of the same support we gave to his predecessors, Commissioners Spicer, Yalden and Fortier.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure to rise in this House this afternoon to support Bill C-22 which I had the privilege to table last week. All members have a clear and pressing responsibility and that is to update every piece of legislation so that it will foster economic growth and prosperity in Canada while ensuring that businesses and consumers are treated fairly.

The amendments before the House represent the fruit of an extensive process of consultation review and reflection with those with a stake in the reforms: governments, business, labour, consumers, financial institutions and the insolvency community.

Mr. Speaker, all members of this House agree that the bankruptcy legislation should foster rehabilitation rather than liquidation and that it should afford consumers better protection. Because of this common vision, I can give the members opposite the same assurance I gave the critics I met with: I shall remain open to any reasonable suggestion concerning changes to be made to the proposed legislation.
Allow me, Mr. Speaker, to outline briefly the contemplated reform. The new legislation will give businesses that have a reasonable chance of surviving the tools to ensure their survival.

We are proposing that the current rules be changed to allow businesses in financial trouble the option of filing a notice of state of 30 days, with the official receiver for protection from all creditors, both unsecured and secured.
Another goal of the proposed reform is to strike a new balance between the following: the rights of the unpaid suppliers, the Crown interests and personal bankruptcies.
Everyone in this House will certainly be happy to hear that the primary purpose of the new provisions concerning the rights of the unpaid suppliers is the well-being of small businesses. All too often, in a single customer context, a flourishing business would collapse over a single deal when a shipment could not delivered because the business it was intended for had declared bankruptcy.
So, from now on, within 30 days of the delivery of goods to a business which is subsequently placed under receivership or declared bankrupt, suppliers will be entitled to reposess the goods.
We also took steps to limit the priority of the Crown, one of the more blatantly unfair aspect of the present Bankruptcy Act.
We have not forgotten consumers in the reform. Under the current rules, individuals cannot effectively negotiate with their creditors on amounts owing. This is unfair to both debtors and creditors. That is why we will permit the repayment period to be extended and permit debtors to negotiate with their creditors on amounts owed.
In the same vein, our reforms will make it less difficult for bankrupt individuals to get back on their feet by proposing to streamline guidelines governing access to summary administration.
Mr. Speaker, everyone has been saying for the longest time that one of the most serious deficiencies of the Bankruptcy Act, as it stands, is the fact that it does not protect the people who work for businesses that go bankrupt. In such cases, not only do the workers loose their jobs but, all too often, they never see a penny of the back wages their employer owed them. That is why we are proposing a new wage claim program to give them some protection as regards the payment of their wages and vacation pay upon their employer declaring bankruptcy or being placed under receivership.



June 19, 1991



-to be funded from employer contributions of roughly 10 cents per employee per week.
The program will allow employees in an employer's bankruptcy, receivership or liquidation to receive up to $2,000 for wages and vacation pay, and up to an additional $1,000 for unpaid expenses for travelling sales people.
The federal government, the largest employer in the country, will pay into the program as well, and we have asked provincial governments to do likewise.
To minimize the paper burden of employers, premiums will be collected jointly with the unemployment insurance program.
Finally, we have also included in this act a provision for it to be reviewed by Parliament after three years. We must never again allow so important a piece of legislation to become as seriously out-dated as the Bankruptcy Act.

Mr. Speaker, preparing this reform was a real challenge because we had to strike the right balance between protecting the interests of small businesses, consumers and wage-earners on the one hand and, on the other, helping viable businesses get back on their feet and protect jobs.
Mr. Speaker, I believe the reform I put before this House will help us reach those goals. I ask all honourable members for their support so that Bill C-22 is enacted as soon as possible. Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind this House that in 1987, the last time a bill numbered C-22 was tabled in this House by the present Government House Leader who was then Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, that bill on the drug industry was a resounding success. I hope 22 will be a lucky number again. We trust that, with the cooperation of my colleagues in this House, we will be able to pass this bill quickly at this stage. We will refer it to committee for preliminary study, so that, come September and October, we will be in a position to pass it in this House so that we may enjoy the benefits of this legislation very soon next fall.

Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of pleasure that I rise today to speak to
Government Orders
this motion which deals with the disposition and the treatment of Bill C-22 in that it would allow Bill C-22 and its contents to be pre-studied by the consumer and corporate affairs committee prior to its introduction and debate at second reading in the House.
I think it is fair to say that after some consultation with the minister who just spoke, I would have to be in agreement that the timing of this bill is important. The Bankruptcy Act has not had substantial amendments applied to it since 1966. The current bankruptcy legislation which we are operating under has been around since 1949.
There are a number of provisions in that act which have to be scuttled. There are some new provisions which have to be added. There is some updating which certainly has to be done. Some of the major components of the act lead me to believe that with some flexibility on the side of the government, and it is there because I think it truly has a desire to come up with a piece of legislation which is workable and supportable by all those who are concerned, during the pre-study period we will certainly be able to listen to interested groups.
It is my hope that the committee will be able to travel as we do the pre-study, not extensively, but as much as necessary to listen to those parties that are interested outside of the capital region. Bankruptcies do not just happen here, they happen all over the country. If good suggestions come forward in the spirit of co-operation and compromise, I hope the government will listen to that and will accept good amendments that do not alter the direction of the act.
Concerning the direction of the act itself, there are two or three points which I just want to very briefly address.
The Wage Earner Protection Program is one which is long since overdue, and is one which has been the subject in the past of some private member's motions in this House. Back in 1949, there was a provision for some priority for workers' wages up to an amount of $500. The effect of this Bill C-22 would put in place a fund for workers' wages to a maximum of $2,000, plus the $1,000 for sales persons' expenses would come out of the fund. The government thinks that this may cost abut $60 million per year. It is proposed under that piece of legislation to be financed solely by the employers.

We have some difficulty with that for a couple of reasons, which we will get into during the course of the debate, and which I am sure will be raised by interested parties which will be called upon to submit testimony during the pre-study period.
One of the questions we want to examine and talk to individuals about is whether the wage earner protection fund actually should have been in two parts. One fund with a super priority for wages and the second fund, financed either by the Treasury or by a combination of an employer tax and the Treasury of the Government of Canada, which would basically act as the emergency fund but still give super priority.
Those are things about which we will listen to witnesses to determine if the current proposal is the best one for the circumstances.
Another provision which is very timely and overdue deals with the 30 day stay provision for firms in financial difficulty. It is absolutely essential that this type of protection, which they have had in the United States for a number of years, is introduced to a modern bankruptcy act in Canada.
As we all know, because we all have constituents who are in business, all too often secured creditors walk in quickly, seize assets, cut off credit lines, and put receivers in place. Many times healthy companies, for whatever reason-they may be having some temporary difficulty-find themselves in a position where they cannot go on with their business and bankruptcy ensues. The purpose of any amendment to the Bankruptcy Act, as the minister said, is to instil some balance in the system, balance between all the players in business, without any question.
We must ensure that this 30 day provision is sufficient to protect the interest of the debtor, of the consumer and of the secured creditors. Those things will be debated.
One of the other provisions which is extremely important deals with suppliers. All too often what happens is that suppliers, who basically lend, give material to other businesses and perhaps they are out 30 or 60 days. A day or two after the material, perhaps large amounts, go to
another business that business will declare bankruptcy and most of the time the supplier is not in a secured position. Unfortunately, the supplier loses a tremendous amount of money and in many cases the domino effect causes that supplier to go out of business. We have seen that a lot in the current recession.
Those provisions are also addressed in the bill. A pre-study of the bill will allow other interested parties to participate and I think we might see some good suggestions for amendments.
The only major concern I have at this point is that we are in a period of record bankruptcies. As we well know, the bankruptcies in the first quarter of this year have been at a near record level. The total number of bankruptcies in the last seven years, since this government took power, is a staggering 273,789. In each of those cases in the case of consumer bankruptcies, there is a great deal of devastation felt by those people who have had to claim bankruptcy under this antiquated act.
As for business bankruptcies, there are hundreds of thousands of individuals who over the last seven years have found themselves in great difficulty with some of the wages, the investment they have put in the company, at risk. I am certainly hoping that those individuals will be able to be heard during the pre-study and have some input into the final package presented to the House, during second reading and when it finally does get to committee after second reading.
One of my big concerns, and I should say it here, is the amount. The ceiling is $2,000. If we simply factor in the $500 protection of the 1949 act with the CPI factor it should be around $3,100 or $3,200.
Again in the Coulter report of 1980, a figure of $2,000 for such protection was suggested. If you factor in the CPI it appears that protection should be around $3,200. Those are the types of concerns that we will be bringing to the pre-study and that I am sure we will hear about.
Again, the big concern we have is that some of the provisions of this act are not going to be enforced. If the act was passed today, we would still have a problem with the wage earner protection program.

The wage earner protection program cannot be put in force until January 1, 1992, which means that even if this House could find some consensus right now, there would still be hundreds of thousands of individuals, if the current recession and record numbers of bankruptcies continue, who would not find any protection in that particular fund.
Indeed, the studies have shown that in commercial bankruptcies 30 per cent of them have wage claims that are left outstanding. The sooner that this type of protection is brought in, the better off it will be for thousands of Canadian workers right across this country.
In closing, I hope that by the time this committee gets to do the pre-study in the fall, we will see some signs of recovery, some signs of a change in this government's economic policies which caused this recession in the first place.
I hope that we will not be sitting here in this House in December after this bill is passed, knowing full well that because the bill did not come in earlier in the session and the wage earner protection fund did not kick in earlier, that another 40,000, 30,000 or 25,000 companies and individuals have declared bankruptcy. Mr. Speaker, it has been an interesting 20 minutes. We now start to look at the question of money laundering which Bill C-9 deals with. Bill C-9 is an important piece of legislation which requires financial institutions to keep the various paper records which will be essential in the tracing of money laundering operations associated with organized crime.
This attempt to deal with money laundering more effectively is certainly something that we in the New Democratic Party support. We were especially pleased to be able to persuade the government in the course of the previous session of Parliament that it was important in a bill such as this, which leaves so much of the details of what will take place to regulation, to see to it that regulations would not be put into effect until there had been a period of at least 90 days after their publication in the Canada Gazette, during which time people would be able to make presentations to the government with respect to those regulations.
We feel that is an important precedent for future pieces of legislation which have the same reliance on regulations as Bill C-9 does.
We also feel, and I gather that the government is in agreement with us now on this point, that if during that 90-day period there is a change in those regulations which leads to a different set of regulations being put out within that 90-day period for reflection and representation, it shall then be possible still to have a further 30 days for those people who were prepared to accept and to live with the previous regulation to be able to adjust to the regulation change, and to be able to make representations with respect to the change and so on and so forth.
The recommendations which came first to the government for this extended 90-day period and subsequently, were presented to a legislative committee which reviewed this bill, came from the Canadian Bar Association. They represent an important principle in the view of the Bar Association that you should not have regulations put into effect without some period of possibility for dealing with those regulations and responding to those regulations on the part of those who will be affected by the regulations.
We would have preferred to move this particular amendment at the legislative committee stage, but some mix-ups in communication at that stage made it impossible to do so and so we have moved it at report stage on the basis of the representations made to us during the legislative committee hearings by the Canadian Bar Association. It felt this legislation should not proceed without this further 30-day period if there is a change in regulations as a consequence of representations during the 90-day period allowed with respect to the original regulations set out.
With this change, which I understand the government is prepared to accept, there is the possibility that it will be moving a subamendment which will put this particular amendment into conformity with the original piece of legislation; making it 90 days as opposed to 95 days. We would support and accept this change. We think that this now represents a good piece of legislation.
It is a piece of legislation which will make it easier for our police forces to deal with money laundering associated with drug trafficking and with other forms of money laundering. We think it is an important step for the government to be taking. We are pleased that step is being taken as part of a broad series of moves on the part of various countries throughout the world to try to get better control over money laundering in order to deal with the serious problems which it represents and which drug trafficking represents to our society, to our children, and to the world itself.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. friend for his concern.
As I was saying earlier, money laundering is the process by which illegal profits are transformed through financial markets into legitimate funds serving to obscure the real identity of the real owners of the funds and to obscure the nature and the source of these funds.
These activities are being pursued on an international scale and there has been a move afoot in the G-7 and other international forums to develop domestic programs and encourage co-operation to combat this program.
There is little question that a fundamental part of any attempt to control and combat the smuggling of illegal drugs must be the development of effective monitoring and evidence gathering systems in the laundering of drug profits.
There has been general consensus in this country for some time that there are great shortcomings in Canada's financial reporting laws. It has been because of these shortcomings, coupled with our proximity to major drug routes and our large, open border with the United States, that Canada has gained a reputation world-wide as an easy and safe place to launder the profits of illegal activities.

In testimony to the legislative committee studying the bill before us, RCMP officials confirmed that the problem of money laundering in Canada has indeed been a large one. In fact, over $1 billion a year is laundered in Canada through illegal drug practices.
What this has meant is that police agencies, once having identified someone believed to be engaged in criminal activities, were severely hampered in the collection of evidence that might help convict these people. As such, we are very eager on this side of the House for this government to bring down legislation that will correct these matters.
After the disappointment with the government's first attempt in the last session with Bill C-89, we are considerably more satisfied with the bill before us today. We are pleased that the government has given consideration to the shortcomings of the previous bill brought to the attention of this House by members on this side of the House.
The draft regulations accompanying the bill are also an improvement. There are now definitions of cash and of the nature of the records that must be kept. There is still some concern however in our party that too much is left to regulation. As such, the operation of this legislation could change dramatically without being brought before this House, again requiring only an Order in Council.
We do understand the need as was articulated in the committee for flexibility in such a moving area. We recognize that, as many people are engaged in money laundering activities, they are very quick to find and exploit any loophole in the law. We must be just as quick to stop them from doing this.
There also remains a concern that the recording of large transactions will be extended to overseas branches of Canadian banks. We know, for instance, that there is a significant amount of money laundering activity going on in the Caribbean. It is our hope that this will not provide for the significant undermining of our efforts. We are pleased that more countries are joining the effort to curb laundering activities at this time.
I will leave it at that, but I would just like to leave you with a note. We want to send a message to this government and to the people who would do these illegal activities in our country. We as parliamentarians will not stand for this.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise for a few moments to speak on Bill C-2. As members know, my constituency is the constituency of Calgary West.
For some time now one of the smaller units of the National Energy Board has been located in the riding of Calgary West and in fact is housed at the present time in the same building as my constituency office.
This piece of legislation in terms of western Canada, the provinces of Alberta and Calgary in particular, has symbolic significance of great importance. We lived through a very difficult time some years ago with the National Energy Program which had some very difficult consequences for our community and our part of the country. That is where the symbolism comes in, the transfer of the National Energy Board to Calgary has a symbolic flavour.
Perhaps of more importance in the longer term is the fact that it will reduce the costs consumers ultimately have to pay for the provision of energy in this country. The location of the board in the city of Calgary really signifies the fact that 90 per cent of the work done by the board and those who are petitioners before the board involve firms in the city of Calgary. This will cut down enormously on their travel costs, food costs, airline tickets and so on, and ultimately any business expense ends up being paid for by consumers.
This move, while a bit costly in its initial phase, will have long-term consequences over the decades and will reduce those costs to the consumers of the future. It is a sound business proposition. It has symbolic importance,
particularly in this year when we are so engaged and will be engaged in the 12 months ahead on national unity issues. That symbolic importance for the good of this nation through its willingness to stay together cannot be underestimated. I guess if there is a negative side to it, we know and we feel badly for some of the families that feel they cannot travel to Calgary. It would be lovely if they could. They would enjoy it and their children would prosper in that part of the world, but there are families with two incomes, with two jobs and there are difficulties in many cases caused to families in the Ottawa region.
The provisions to assist those people in securing employment with the Government of Canada in this region are also an important part of the plan of the government so that the disruption to families is minimized as much as possible.
In closing, I just want to say to the National Energy Board on behalf of the people who live in my riding, the people who live in my city, the people who live in my province and the people who live in western Canada, welcome, we will treat you well. The country will be better off when this piece of legislation is proclaimed.

Mr. Speaker, I know it is getting late but I really did need to speak on this bill. I have just been through the rather unpleasant and difficult experience of sitting on the legislative committee on Bill C-2 and it was once again a demonstration that the government is prepared to use its majority power either in the House or in committee to override any sense of good democratic process.
The government has had this bill in hand in committee since May 23, 1991.
It was only last week, over three weeks later, on June 18 that the committee finally convened to consider who it would invite as witnesses. Having sat on the bill for three weeks, the government members on the committee used their majority to ensure that the committee would complete its business less than 48 hours later. What it essentially said was there are witnesses who want to be heard from, but unless they can come to its beck and call within the next 36 hours, the committee is not going to hear from them.
As a result, many of those employees to whom the member just referred, who are affected by this decision of the government to move the National Energy Board, were unable to appear either individually or through their union representative and present their concerns about this bill, some suggestions which they felt should be considered by the government and possibly even in the legislation.
There was ample time for the committee to hear from witnesses and conclude its business in time for this House to deal with this bill before the recess. However, members were adamant that they would not sit at all on a Friday or on Thursday evening or on Monday to hear from people whose lives are being disrupted and changed with very little warning and very little notice.
The committee was able to hear, excuse me, chose to hear from only one representative of employees representing the small component, the Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada. The Energy, Mines and Resources component of the Public Service Alliance of Canada, the Council of Canadians and numerous others that had written to the minister indicating their interests
Government Orders
in this bill and their opposition to this bill were not allowed to come before the legislative committee.
Many of my own constituents could have come had the committee in time given any indication, had the government members of the committee in time given any indication that they would not hear from the duly elected union representatives of those employees. They did not, and therefore people were denied the opportunity to present to the members of this Parliament their concerns and ways in which those concerns could have been remedied.
There is a lot of playing with words in this. It was very interesting during the course of discussions to find out that this government has no decentralization policy. It was very interesting to find out that it does but it does not. We asked very specifically, and the information I have from the Treasury Board is this: "The decentralization program no longer exists." The decentralization policy does not apply. On the other hand, the next paragraph says: "For some time the Treasury Board has been working to eliminate the decentralization policy".
You may ask: what difference does this make to this bill and to these employees? The change in location of the National Energy Board affects over 300 employees. If this were being handled properly, as the decentralization should be, the employees would be given up to a year's notice of their move. They would be given an extended period of time in which to maintain a residence here, travel back and forth, and adjust their family life to their new situation.
Because the policy is not being followed by this government, people are being forced to make choices to either separate their families or not move with the board. The result is that the board is losing some very competent and capable people. I think that is a shame, but I think it is more of a shame that the federal government is not living by its own policy, which says one year notice to employees.
We all know that this has been extremely rushed and as a result it is extremely expensive, and I will come to that in a moment. The announcement was made in the budget on February 26 without the knowledge of the chairman of the board of the National Energy Board and without, I am told, the knowledge of the minister. As late as the end of April people did not know the conditions under which they were being asked to move, they did not know what expenses would be paid or what would await them in Calgary, but they were asked to make a decision within less than three weeks as to whether they wished to uproot their family and move halfway across the country. That is not a fair and just way to treat people.

June 19, 1991
Government Orders
The minister, when he appeared before the committee, referred to fair and equitable treatment of all employees. I want to acknowledge that the minister seemed genuinely surprised when he found out that all employees were not being treated equally and were not being treated fairly, that some employees in the management category were being treated with much more compassion, with much more respect and with very special privileges compared to the rest of the employees of the National Energy Board.
I urged the minister during the hearings, and I urge him again, to ensure that the equity and fairness he referred to in his presentation to the committee are respected and that people are treated with compassion and concern for their individual lives.
Unfortunately, the minister chose to use the opportunity to make some rather unfortunate comments about public servants and I want to refer to them because I do not think that was appropriate. The attitude on the other side of the House seems to be that if people choose not to go with the Energy Board it is because they are not loyal to their employer or because they somehow have something against Calgary. Nothing could be further from the truth.
People have reasons why they are unable to relocate when a government job relocates. It is entirely inappropriate for the minister to say things like: "To put it bluntly, I have very little time for public servants who, with emphasis on service, somehow feel it is their great gift to the Canadian public if they are located in Ottawa". That is not the case at all. People were hired here. They have established families here. There were many particular cases we heard over the course of the hearings which indicate why people will choose not to move.
The kind of special treatment the management category is getting is very effective because 75 per cent of the management category is going while-and I think this should be a real concern-only one-third of the scientific and technical category is going and less than 10 per cent of some of the support staff.
That very clearly indicates that this move has a discriminatory and much more significant effect on women employees of the board, and I think the board needs to address that.
The other concern is the move to special employer status. Unfortunately the chair of the committee ruled out of order an addition to the bill which would have protected employees during the transition to special employer status. Again I urge the minister, having not agreed to that amendment so it could be incorporated in the bill, to have a look at truly meeting the obligation of fairness to employees of the board, as he stated.
The member who spoke previously said that this will save money. In fact it will cost $26 million and there has been no cost benefit study done, so he has no way of knowing whether it will save money or whether it will cost more money. It will definitely cost more money to hire employees. The board will have to pay up to $15,000 extra for many of their employees to compete with the market in Calgary, and that is the reason for applying for special employer status.
I would encourage the member to stick to the facts, to withdraw any suggestion that he knows this will save money, when he knows no such thing. In fact, the cost is $26 million, some of which will be paid by the industry. However, as the member has said, that portion will end up on the oil, gas or coal bill of every consumer in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I would just like to say, first of all, that I share the concerns of the member for Ottawa West. Second, I have nothing significant to add to the remarks I made at second reading or to the remarks made by my colleague, the member for Nanaimo-Cowichan at second reading. The concerns we have for the employees of the board stand. However, on balance we support the bill.

"Key statistics on Federal Public Service Work Force, 1990"

And this tells us that, in 1990, all these 218,328 employees were proportionally distributed according to the population of each province. In the discussions with the Public Service, we are also reminded that they are trying to reach a proportion which would be fair for women, men and visible minorities. Two hundred and seventy-three civil servants will be asked to leave the national capital region, Mr. Speaker. I am wondering what for. Thirty per cent of these civil servants are French-speaking people who live either on the Quebec or on the Ontario side. These families will now be forced to live in Calgary, a wonderful place which is extremely friendly, I have been there. I know some people and I have friends who work there. However, the majority of the people who work in Calgary-I would even say practically everybody at the present time-are people who really want to live in Calgary and make it their home. But presently, some families are going to be torn apart.
Several civil servants belong to families where both husband and wife are working. They both work to pay for their home, their mortgage and all the family related expenses. What protection is the government going to offer in the case an employee who is moved to Calgary if his or her spouse cannot find a job? What protection? None. In the case of children, are there any French schools? I am told that yes, there are some. Will they have access to professional legal services in French? Will they have a French community centre? Will they be able to live in French, if they want to?
Families will be torn apart, Mr. Speaker. government does. The two motions deal with the following points. There are really three points embodied in the two motions. The first important point is that the first amendment would provide that the government will be bound by very specific criteria when it comes to consider adding countries to the Automatic Firearms Country Control List. Bill C-6 gives to the Governor in Council the right to establish an Automatic Firearms Country Control List, the result of which is that automatic firearms can then be exported to that country.
There is in place now a government policy that covers export permits in respect of weapons and military goods. The government has said in committee-and the hon. Minister for International Trade said it in committee- that the government would be bound by the polity which has been established by the government in deciding whether or not it is going to permit the export of automatic weapons. This amendment embodies precisely the requirements that the government says it will be bound by. Rather than leave it to the government, this amendment would have Parliament control the criteria applicable to adding countries to the list. The great significance of this is that we have here a very critical national policy as to whether we are going to get into the arms trade business with countries outside NATO and countries with which we have traditionally traded arms.
Saudi Arabia is the first in a slippery slope. There is a risk that governments will be tempted, for industrial policy reasons, to begin trading with Indonesia, South Korea, the Philippines, South Africa, who knows what countries, in the interests of furthering the industrial concerns of various constituencies. These criteria will prevent a government from changing, at whim, the policies that it wishes to follows, and we call on the government to consent and agree to that.
The second part of the amendment imposes a requirement that the list be approved by the House of Commons, that the list be made public and open to public debate. It would seem to me that the reasons for that are self-evident, because of what the government calls an anomaly in the Criminal Code. The government is being forced out in the open to debate the sale of light armoured vehicles, with automatic weapons attached, to Saudi Arabia. That debate has been very valuable, as we will see shortly. It is critically important, as a matter of public policy, that whenever the Automatic Firearms Country Control List is established, whenever countries are added to it, that that be a matter of public debate in this House and subject to the approval of the House.
The final point, and I will finish now, is that the amendment will require that before an export permit for prohibited weapons is issued, there will be a security impact assessment by a committee of the House of Commons. Again that is self-evident, similar to an environmental impact assessment. We believe that no sales of firearms or other weapons should take place around the world unless it is in the security interests of Canada.
It cannot be merely for the industrial interests of Canada. It must be for the security interests of Canada and consistent with those security interests. The idea of a

Why then are we attempting to put the government's policy into legislation? The reason we are trying to do this, and the reason the hon. member is trying to do this, is that as the legislation is written it is too wide open. Through the legislation alone the government could in fact sell to a number of countries that many of us would not approve of.
For example, the legislation as written says that the government can sell these automatic firearms to any country that is on the Automatic Firearms Country Control List. It says that only those countries with which the government has an agreement for defence, research, development and production, can go on that list. At the present time, the government has 10 such agreements. Nine of the agreements are with NATO countries and the tenth one is with Sweden. At the present time, the government can only sell these automatic firearms to those 10 countries, but not necessarily to those 10 countries.

The problem is that the government can conclude further agreements on defence research and so on with countries and there are no guidelines, no criteria to stop it from developing, let us say, from concluding agreements with countries all around the world, some of whom are involved in conflict, some of whom have serious human rights violations.
The government has a policy-it is not in this legislation-that it will not sell arms or that it will consider very seriously selling arms to countries that are involved in conflict, either international or internal conflict, or it will consider very seriously selling arms to countries that have serious human rights violations.
We think these are good policy criteria, but we want those policy criteria included in the legislation. That is what I attempted to do in committee, and it was defeated by the government members. Now the hon. member is attempting to do the same thing at report stage. I think that is a good thing.
The response of the government, when we tried to do that in committee, was that this would make it too inflexible for. the government. We say that is correct. It will make it too inflexible for the government. Why should the government suddenly want to change its own guidelines which are sound? Why, for example, would the government want to sell weapons to a country where there are serious human rights violations? Why would the government want to change the policy and sell arms to a country that is involved in conflict, either internally or internationally, where the security of Canada is not involved? Why would the government want to sell arms to a country where the United Nations has imposed sanctions, such as South Africa?
We are saying if the government takes these guidelines seriously, and they are sound, then they should not be subject simply to ministerial change in a cabinet room. We are saying that these guidelines are so sound and so reasonable that they should be put in the legislation.
That is what my hon. friend is trying to do. They are not expressed exactly in the same way, but they are substantially the same as the government's policy guidelines. He is putting them in the legislation and, yes, they will make it more inflexible. The government will not be able to change them unless they come back to the House of Commons and seek an amendment. We think that is a good thing, because it puts the control of these very important matters, that is, to whom we sell arms, in the hands of parliamentarians and not simply the cabinet.
The other reason why it is important to put these guidelines in the legislation is because if they are broken, or if they are interpreted too widely, then a
citizen can go to court and seek an injunction saying: "You are breaking the legislative guidelines".
If the guidelines simply are left in a policy document as expressed by the government, by the minister, and they are interpreted too broadly or too loosely or even violated, there is no way anyone can go to court and say to the judge that the government is breaking the guidelines because they are not law. What the hon. member is doing is putting these guidelines into law, and we support that.
One might ask again, why we want to do this at this time when they have been in policy documents for years and years and that has been more or less satisfactory. We want to do it now because there is a new commitment to stopping the sale of arms to countries with serious human rights abuses or who are involved in conflict.
During the Iraq-Kuwait war, the world was outraged by the fact that 95 per cent of the armaments held by Iraq were sold to Iraq by the five permanent members of the Security Council. The Prime Minister of Canada, and rightly so, said he was outraged at that and called for a world summit to control the arms trade. That was seconded by the former Secretary of State for External Affairs, who said that it was very bad that the world should be selling arms to a country like Iraq, especially in such great numbers, and that we must do something about it.
We agree with the government. We agree with the Prime Minister. We agree with the former Minister for External Affairs that something more substantial should be done. What we are suggesting, and I support the hon. member, is that we put these guidelines into law and I hope the House will accept that.
