Mr. Speaker, I trust that most of the members of the House will remain while I explain to them why they should vote against this bill on third reading. I am sure that they know the reasons why they should be against this bill. It is those opposite who should remain while we are doing this. Perhaps we could have a second while the House clears.
We have 30 minutes in which to address the issue of the fundamentals of this bill. What I would like to do is first of all set out the two fundamental reasons why our party is against this bill and will vote against it on third reading.
The first is fundamentally a matter of conscience. This bill will permit the sale of automatic weapons to any country in the world that the government deems fit to sell those-

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order, please. I would ask the cooperation of both sides of the House. I would remind hon. members they are invited to a reception given by the Speaker at the usual place.

I recognize again the hon. member from Victoria.

The minister of privatization or whatever it is, says he is going for a drink. That would probably help his understanding. The member chose to intervene in the debate. The minister chose to heckle during the debate. There is no order in that point. It seems to me
that if the government members are interested in listening, I hope they will just learn a point of two from the observations we have to make.
This is one of the most important policy initiatives that is before the House in this part of the session. It represents a significant departure of Canadian policy which would permit the sale of automatic weapons to Saudi Arabia. That country has a very poor human rights record. It is in a region of the world which is sensitive, testy and has just come through one of the most difficult wars of this century. The people of that region are still paying the price.
The war that we have seen in the gulf is a war which both sides in this House can see was caused by the uncontrolled sale of arms by the western world to a region which did not need those arms. It seems to me that the first issue is an issue of conscience of all Canadians. I believe that Canadians find it very difficult to understand why it is that one of the first bills that this government introduces in this session is a bill to extend and expand the sale of arms after the eloquent statements which were made at the end of the gulf war.
As we went through this bill and through committee, I learned a thing or two about how the government works. It became very clear that instead of the conspiracy theory of operation it is the screw-up theory that really counts most of the time. This bill was an invention of the international trade side and those who are responsible for selling goods abroad. The export permit people in External Affairs and the trade minister are responsible for this bill, not the External Affairs minister who is responsible for disarmament and arms control, not the Prime Minister, but those who are responsible for industry.
The argument that is made in committee for this bill over and over again is the industrial argument. Here we have jobs. Here we have an industry. Let's sell them. Who cares what the purpose of the weapons are? Who cares that there are people who may be killed as a result of the sale of arms to Saudi Arabia? That is irrelevant.
We had an official from the minister's department who came before our committee and said that the only reason for this bill was industrial. There was no examination of the security reasons for this bill, there was no suggestion of the foreign policy reasons for this bill. What we had was simply a trade deal.
June 19, 1991

Surely, after everything that the world has seen in this century, the time has come to call a halt to arms sales. That is the first issue before the House.
The second issue is that this bill is flawed. The government has said over and over again that it complies with certain standards when it comes to the sale of arms. But its members refuse to agree to an amendment which would incorporate those standards in the legislation. The government has refused amendments which would require it to make the list of countries public to whom arms will be sold. It has refused those amendments. It has refused sunset clauses. It has refused to set out the reasons why we should be permitting sale of arms abroad. That is the second reason why we are against this bill.
The government was so anxious that this bill go through because there is at least one side of the government's head which understands that the defence industry is fundamentally a flawed industry. Around the world, the market for arms is fading. The third world can no longer afford arms. The market in the west is contracting. The cold war is over and investments which Liberal and Conservative governments have made in the arms industry are proving to be flawed investments.
Yes, hundreds of thousands of jobs.
My Liberal friend here says "Hundreds of thousands of jobs". But it is jobs at the price of human lives.
Give me a break.

He says, "Give me a break". They are making guns, they are making automatic guns which are going to be sold to a repressive regime in Saudi Arabia.
Out of all of this has come at least one ray of hope, and I would like to use the remaining couple of minutes to outline where that ray of hope is coming from.
Last night the government agreed at long last to a suggestion put before our committee by the Canadian Arms Control Centre, John Lamb and Project Ploughshares, that the time had come for a full public review of the export of arms by Canada, the defence production industry and policies of conversion from military uses to
Government Orders
civilian uses. As a result of that agreement, tomorrow morning the external affairs committee will meet and will strike a special subcommittee, which will be authorized and agreed to by all sides of this House, to conduct that public inquiry.
Hear, hear.

That public inquiry will have hearings not only in Ottawa, but outside of Ottawa. We will work in full co-operation with the citizens' inquiry that has been established by the Canadian Peace Alliance and involves groups from all across Canada. We will be working closely with that citizens' inquiry. Members on all sides of the House will work to try to understand that there must be a better way for Canadians to earn their living.
This morning I spoke to CAW Local 27 from the hon. Liberal member's riding. Its members asked for this bill to be passed. They disagree with our position that this bill should be defeated. But they said to me this morning that they, more than any other Canadians, want to earn their living doing something other than making arms. The time has come for members on all sides of this House to realize first, that this is a dying industry. This country cannot continue to go through the slippery slope of first selling to the Americans, then to the Europeans, then to countries like Saudi Arabia. Who will be next? Indonesia? South Korea? South Africa? If the government accedes, as it has in this case, to the argument of selling to Saudi Arabia, it will accede next year to an argument to sell to Indonesia or South Korea or to whatever other dictatorship wants arms from Canada because this is a dying industry.
The first thing the government has to realize and will realize is that there must be a change in how we earn a living.
Let me finish with this note. All Canadians want this Parliament to show some leadership in ending the arms race which has caused so much tragedy around the world. I believe that the agreement the government made last night to establish a public inquiry into Canadian policies in this area is a very important first step toward working out that kind of leadership for this country.

June 19, 1991
Government Orders
I am very pleased that the government has acceded to that. I am very hopeful that the subcommittee will do very useful work for Canadians and that finally, perhaps, we can turn the comer and Canada can truly realize its place in the world as a peacemaker.

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to take long in this debate but I do want to put some perspective on what the hon. from the New Democratic Party has been saying.
To listen to him you would think that one of the major industries, one of the largest industries in this country was the arms industry. This is simply not the case. To listen to him you would expect that we were a major contributor to the build-up of arms in the Middle East which took place prior to the gulf crisis. That is simply not the case.
What I think is very clear is that we have in this legislation listened very carefully to the concerns that people have expressed about the importance of putting tight controls on any arms shipments. As we have moved into the area of the export of automatic weapons, we have been conscious of the fact that there is an anomaly which has prohibited the export of these arms, an anomaly in the Criminal Code which was not contemplated at the time the Criminal Code was changed in 1977. We are correcting that anomaly.
I think it is important to note that as we have corrected this anomaly, we have put a tighter set of export controls on the export of automatic weapons by providing for a country control list which will be very tightly controlled. There are very stringent requirements as to what type of country can be on that list. In addition to that, there will be a case by case review of every arms shipment that will be made that is subject to these restrictions.
There is a long history of control of weapons from this country. This government is not changing that history. It is not trying in any way to make any deviation from the standards and the traditions and values which have been expressed by Canadians during the course of many, many years. Those traditions will be honoured. Those values will be honoured in the administration of the control system that we have put in place.
I do want to make a comment on the statements made by the hon. member to the effect that we are ignoring the fact that there are certain countries, certain areas of
the world which have been subject to excessive arms build-up. We are conscious of that.
The Prime Minister has spoken of that. The previous Secretary of State for External Affairs and the current Secretary of State for External Affairs have spoken to that. We have been at the forefront of encouraging nations, the major arms exporters, to put a more transparent system in place so that we can avoid, as a group of peace loving countries, these build-ups in arms.
I go back to what my friend from the New Democratic Party has said, that the workers of Diemaco or GM Diesel would like to have other jobs so that are not working for a companies that produce arms.
I think that if we lived in an idealistic world, in a utopian world, we could all say that is something we strive for. However, it is simply not a realistic thing that we can expect to achieve in the world we live in today. We have to have armed forces in this country and we have to arm those armed forces so that they can do then-job.
Our level of requirement in this country is simply not sufficient to support domestic industries. What we have put forward in this legislation is a very tightly controlled means by which these companies, which have been suppliers to Canada, can also broaden their markets and supply to other countries and, by so doing, keep a viable arms industry within this country for our domestic needs as they are required. That is the simple basis on which we have allowed a very tightly controlled export, a process, a mechanism by which these arms can be exported to other countries.
If we are going to live in the real world, if we are going to recognize the reality as it is today, we must have some basis of supplying our own domestic needs. We must provide these companies with a basis whereby they can be viable enterprises or else we simply will not be able to have them supplying our needs and we will be totally reliant on the supplies from other countries. I do not think that is a sensible policy.
This is the basis on which we have gone forward. I have not heard much criticism of the mechanisms that we have put in place because they are among the tightest in the world today. It is on this basis that we present this legislation to the House.
June 19, 1991

As I said, we believe that it honours the traditions and values that Canadians have set forward, and we will continue to do so in the implementation of the policies that we have established.

Mr. Speaker, we are now debating the final stage in Bill C-6, which authorizes the sale of automatic firearms to other countries.
The minister, in the speech which he just gave, is pretending that this bill does not open up, to a greater extent, the sale of arms to other countries, but he says that it in fact places greater restrictions on the sale of arms. That is complete nonsense. This bill authorizes the sale of automatic firearms to other countries, firearms that, up until now, are not authorized to be sold to other countries.
This bill in fact authorizes a wider and greater sale of armaments to other countries at a time when the whole world, including the Prime Minister and the former Secretary of State for External Affairs and the present Secretary of State for External Affairs have said we should cut back on the sale of arms to other countries.
I just listened to the television news at 10 o'clock and at the CSCE meetings, which are taking place in Berlin, the present Secretary of State for External Affairs tried to convince the ministers of other countries that they should cut back the sale of arms to other countries. I could not believe what I was hearing since this bill is before this House tonight.
Let us read again what the Prime Minister said on February 8, 1991 in the midst of the Iraq-Kuwait war. He said: "One of the main lessons to be learned from this war is the danger to us all of the proliferation of both conventional and non-conventional weapons." He went on to say: "The major arms exporting firms and nations have contributed to the current crisis."-that is the Iraq-Kuwait crisis-"The greater majority of weapons in Iraq's arsenal come from suppliers in the countries of the five permanent members of the Security Council. This problem must be brought under control and the time to act is now." He went on to say: "Next week I will propose to the UN Secretary-General, Mr. Perez de Cuellar, that the United Nations convene a global summit on the
Government Orders
instruments of war and weapons of mass destruction." That is the Prime Minister on February 8,1991 only a few months ago.
What did the Secretary of State for External Affairs say? He said: "It is imperative that the world declare that there be no Middle East arms bazaar. Ninety-five per cent of the weapons in the hands of Saddam Hussein came from the five permanent members of the Security Council." He went on to say that he would call for a world summit to control the arms trade. There was such outrage at the time of the Iraq-Kuwait war at the fact that 95 per cent of Iraq's armaments came from the five permanent members of the Security Council, that the world said: "Let's do something about this". I thought they were serious. That was one of the few occasions I applauded the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
What do we get a few months later but a bill to authorize the sale from Canada of armaments that up until now had not been possible to sell. We opposed this bill at second reading because it was too open-ended. We can understand the sale of armaments to countries who are involved in collective security arrangements with us for defensive purposes or for peacekeeping. Consequently, I have no argument with the sale of these small arms to the Netherlands and to certain restricted countries. But this bill was too open-ended and lacked parliamentary control, too much control was in the hands of the cabinet and the minister.
At committee I proposed two amendments. One would have restricted the sale of arms in this bill to the very policy criteria that the government has in its policy statement on this matter. The government does have a policy statement on this matter. The problem is that it is not legislated, and if we take the words of the Prime Minister to heart, the words he said in February, and the words the former Secretary of State said in February, then we should make our rules a little bit tougher. We would make them a little bit tougher if we put the guidelines, if we put the policy principles they have in that policy statement, into law. That is what I tried to do in committee and it was defeated by the government members.

June 19, 1991
Government Orders
Tonight the hon. member for Victoria tried to do it again. He had more or less the same ideas in his amendments and it was defeated once again tonight.
The other thing we tried to do was provide for greater transparency in the sale of these arms within our own country. I had put forward an amendment stating that any addition to the list of eligible countries to which we could sell these armaments, each time an addition was proposed by the government, that matter would have to be referred to the standing committee on external affairs where the minister would have to go and justify the addition of this new country for the sale of arms. The committee would discuss it and vote on it and then send that back to the House.
This would put this very important matter, i.e. the sale of arms to other countries, not only in the hands of the back room of the cabinet but also into a committee of Parliament where it could be reviewed.
I recognize that the government has the majority on parliamentary committees and in this House so if it really wanted to ram through the sale of arms to a certain country it would be able to do so. Nevertheless, the Canadian public would see what is happening, and the government would have to come to justify the sale of arms to this new country or other new countries.
My amendment to that effect was defeated in committee, and tonight the amendment of the member for Victoria which was similar was also defeated in this House.
It is difficult to believe that the world, and this government, should show so much outrage at the sale of arms during the Iraq-Kuwait war, and they have forgotten about it so quickly. As a matter of fact, in the speech given by the Secretary of State for External Affairs in London during that war, he pointed out that 28 western northern countries sold arms to both sides. What an obscenity. Of the countries that were not involved in the conflict, 28 of them sold arms to both sides and kept that war going for nine years, and a million people were killed.
They were not Canadians, Americans, French, British, or Russians. They were young Iranians and young Iraqis. They were human beings and these countries made profits, made money, out of selling arms to both sides. I must say that Canada was not one of those 28 countries. We did not sell to either side.
The fact of the matter is that the arms trade is out of control. One does not bring it to a stop, one does not make speeches to the CSCE, as the Secretary of State did today, it seems.
You do not make those speeches and then support a bill at home providing for a greater sale of armaments.
The government did not accept the improvements to the bill which we suggested. It did not accept the amendments we suggested, so we will vote against it again at third reading.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to finally be able to contribute to this debate on Bill C-6 that will authorize the exporting, importing, manufacturing, buying or selling of or other dealing with certain weapons. It is the height of hypocrisy to hear the government say those kinds of things to Canadians at a time when they are outraged by what is happening, particularly in the Gulf region. In January and February, we heard the Prime Minister denounce the arms trade around the world. A few weeks later, the same government members come before the House of Commons and want to contribute to the arms race themselves.
Mr. Speaker, I cannot understand why Canada would accept to militarize its economy today. The reasons given by the Minister for International Trade are not valid. They say they want to make the military industry in Canada more profitable and, for that, we have to export more arms.
Mr. Speaker, I cannot imagine a minister coming to tell this House that to prevent the exporting of arms is not normal. He did say that it was an odd provision of the Criminal Code.
After recent events, I cannot believe that this government, who tried to come across as uncompromising, will join the list of countries who participate fully and freely in the arms race. If Canadians were consulted on this legislation, they would not accept their government authorizing the selling of arms, specially behind everybody's back, because after this House has voted tonight, there will be no more control by Parliament. From now on, it will be External Affairs officers together with National Defence officers and Cabinet ministers who will decide where, when and how we will sell arms. I do not understand why there is no parliamentary control on a matter of such importance, Mr. Speaker.
June 19, 1991

Government Orders
The hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace talked about his amendments that we supported, but we cannot accept the fact that we are giving a blank cheque to this government to sell arms all over the world. We just have to look at recent events, not only around the world, but in the province of Quebec. Everybody wants a stricter control of arms. Everywhere, people want to restrain this epidemic of violence. Today, the government wants us to believe there will be a stricter control of firearms. We know how the government is. We know what lobby is putting pressure on them, Mr. Speaker. The legislation before the House is certainly the product of the defense industry's lobby. This industry successfully lobbied the Conservatives who now put cost effectiveness before human dignity.
I cannot believe it, Mr. Speaker, when I hear these people say, as they did even today, that they are willing to sell arms to some countries, which have no democratic principles and-no respect whatsoever for human rights and for the fundamental values Canadians and Quebecers all share, especially where peace is concerned. If there is one thing our conscience dictates to all of us, it is our quest for peace on earth.
Canadians are always sad to see their government sell its soul in order to sell arms.
Mr. Speaker, this is unprecedented, and only a Conservative government would introduce such a piece of legislation.
Eleven per cent in the polls.

No wonder they are so low in the polls. Their policies go against the best interests of Canadians, but especially against their consciences. Today, they gave us the most striking example of that.
First, they followed blindly all military decisions made by the Americans and then they were ordered by somebody to impose this kind of bill to this House.
Mr. Speaker, the Bloc Quebecois will fight this bill tooth and nail. It is too bad this government does not have more of a conscience.

hon. member for Windsor West, to say a few words, but since he is temporarily absent from the House, it is my pleasure to thank first of all the pages who will be leaving us.
I will not look at them, because I think we are all very sad to see them go.

It is a custom that at the very end, someone gets up. It is too bad somebody else did not do it. These young people are our hope for the Canada of tomorrow we wish to see.
Hear, hear.

I sometimes stay longer in politics because when I see these young people who will be the Canada of tomorrow, I think there is hope.
There is one thing which I hope-I say it in English only-that they have understood. There are, in this House, many different kinds of members of Parliament. There are some who are very devoted to other opinions than mine. I think there is hope that these young people may communicate to their friends and parents that there is a hope for Canada as long as we accept-

-the difference that exists. They have seen it today during this debate. And vive la difference!
